title: X will now tell users when governments have forced it to limit their posts
snippet: X is expanding its “Under the Hood” transparency tool to show when posts have been downranked or withheld in response to local laws and government demands, including which country made the request.
fullText:
X on Monday announced it will now tell users when their posts have been “shadowbanned,” meaning shown to fewer people, due to the company’s compliance with local laws. The feature is an expansion of the social network’s earlier transparency tool called “Under the Hood,” which allows users to see if any labels have been applied to their account or their posts that could have affected their visibility on the platform.

It will also highlight any downranking of users’ posts due to government-required content filtering.

We’ve expanded Under The Hood after seeing people’s appreciation of more transparency into government-required content filtering.

In addition to showing labels applied to your account and posts in the prior month, Under The Hood now shows if your account or posts had their… https://t.co/Op5rBnE1jg pic.twitter.com/ZUrbkO28ay

— X Open Source (@XOpenSource) September 19, 2026

Previously, information about how an X user’s account or posts were being labeled and downranked was not available to end users. As a result, many often accused the company, formerly known as Twitter, of having shadowbanned them.

In addition, most companies that share data about government requests do so on an aggregate basis through “transparency reports,” not at the account or post level. 

That began to change when, in August, X rolled out its transparency tool to offer more visibility into its moderation decisions. The “Under the Hood” option in the X app settings allows anyone who has posted at least 10 times during the month to download their aggregate stats as a JSON file, a standard data format. (Non-technical users can drop the file into any AI chatbot to have it explained.)

This same process will now show if an account or posts have had their visibility limited because X is complying with local laws. The file will also include which posts were withheld in a country following a legal demand, and which country made the request.

Governments cite a range of reasons for such demands, from laws against hate speech to terrorism-related content to election rules. Of course, critics, including free-expression groups, say some countries also use these laws to squash political dissent.

The update follows a number of other transparency-related efforts at X, including the open-sourcing of its “For You” algorithm, which selects the posts in users’ main feed, and an expansion of its efforts to open source parts of its codebase. The latter involved adding more detail, including on the model configuration, filtering, and core ranking system details. That means the code now includes the parameters used to weight different signals — information that is key to understanding which posts are actually displayed.

At the time of that open-sourcing effort, X’s vice president of product, Keith Coleman, said it was “the kind of thing that I think people will be fairly shocked that we are releasing.”

title: Here are 100+ things Siri AI can do on your iPhone
snippet: iOS 27 launched this week with the all-new Siri AI. David Pogue put the new Siri to the test by trying 125 requests, here’s how it went. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launched this week with the all-new Siri AI. David Pogue put the new Siri to the test by trying 125 requests, here’s how it went.

iOS 27’s new Siri AI impresses David Pogue following 125 tests

Siri has been baked into the iPhone for nearly 15 years. But during that time, many Apple users have grown accustomed to only depending on Siri for certain supported tasks.

For example, I’ve long relied on Siri to create reminders, start timers, play Apple Music, and when driving I’ll use it to send messages. Outside of those few limited tasks though, Siri’s shortcomings have trained me to not rely on it.

But iOS 27’s new Siri AI is a huge upgrade that can do so much more than ever before. It might just take some time to adjust to it being your go-to, though.

That’s why I found David Pogue’s new Substack post so helpful. Titled “125 Tests of the New AI Siri,” Pogue lists out over 100 prompts he’s tried with Siri AI and details how the assistant did.

Here are a few examples that stood out to me:

28. What are people waiting on me for? (Generates list from Mail, Messages, and Reminders. Incredible. Everything I did for this column was supposed to be for testing purposes only, but this one actually found stuff I’d forgotten I was supposed to do!) […]

30. (Running late to a party:) What’s the apartment number!? (“The apartment number for the Bynum party tonight is 10-F.” Note: I never said what party or what day!) […]

46. Delete all my alarms. (“Do you want to delete 38 alarms in Clock?” Tap to confirm.)

With almost every one of the 125 tests, Siri succeeded. And among the few failures, such as sending a Venmo payment, Siri AI will likely perform better after third parties update their apps for iOS 27 and Siri AI compatibility. 

You can read the full list of 125 Siri AI examples here on Pogue’s Substack.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max still uses a Qualcomm modem in the US, teardown confirms
snippet: TechInsights has published one of the first in-depth iPhone 18 Pro Max teardowns. Most notably, the teardown confirms that the iPhone 18 Pro Max sold in the United States still uses a Qualcomm modem. more…
fullText:
TechInsights has published one of the first in-depth iPhone 18 Pro Max teardowns. Most notably, the teardown confirms that the iPhone 18 Pro Max sold in the United States still uses a Qualcomm modem.

On its tech specs website, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro uses the Apple C2 cellular modem. In every country other than the United States, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max also uses its C2 cellular modem.

The company, however, doesn’t specify which modem the U.S. variant of the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses. Speculation suggested the iPhone 18 Pro Max used a Qualcomm modem, and this teardown confirms it.

According to the TechInsights teardown, the iPhone 18 Pro Max variant sold in the United States uses the Qualcomm Snapdragon X80 modem. This is the same modem used worldwide in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.

So, to recap, here’s how Apple’s transition to its own in-house modem technology has played out in the United States specifically:

iPhone 16 / 16 Plus / 16 Pro / 16 Pro Max: Qualcomm Snapdragon X71

iPhone 16e: Apple C1

iPhone 17 / 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max: Qualcomm X80

iPhone Air: Apple C1X

iPhone 17e: Apple C1X

iPhone 18 Pro: Apple C2

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Qualcomm X80

iPhone Duo: Apple C2

Apple touts that the C2 brings “AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability.” In comparison to the C1X, Apple says the C2 delivers “meaningfully faster uploads when compared to C1X while consuming 15 percent less energy.” The C2 modem also supports mmWave 5G, unlike the C1 and C1X.

It seems clear to me that Apple has caught up to Qualcomm, now that the C2 supports mmWave 5G connectivity. Apple’s C-series modems have always been more power-efficient than Qualcomm’s (which, I’d wager, is something most people care more about than raw download and upload speeds).

Apple hasn’t said why the iPhone 18 Pro Max still uses a Qualcomm modem. The likely explanation, though, is that the decision is purely contractual, and Apple will ditch Qualcomm once and for all as soon as it can.

title: Waymo is offering transit discounts again, this time with Visa
snippet: Waymo has made several attempts over the years at offering transit discounts to its customers in the hopes of getting them to more frequently use the company's robotaxis to connect with a train or a bus. fullText:
Waymo has made several attempts over the years at offering transit discounts to its customers in the hopes of getting them to more frequently use the company’s robotaxis to connect with a train or a bus. The Alphabet-owned company announced the latest effort today, teaming up with Visa to offer a discount on robotaxi rides when they use Waymo to connect with transit.

The new incentive is being rolled out first to customers in the San Francisco-Bay Area. When riders use a Visa credit card to take a Waymo trip and public transit within 2 hours of each other, the company will automatically put a $2.85 credit on their account that can be applied to future Waymo rides.

It’s a similar program to one Waymo tested out in San Francisco in 2024, and in Los Angeles in 2025. The difference now is the involvement of Visa, which allows Waymo to verify when its customers are paying for robotaxi rides and transit trips in close proximity to one another.

The program is modeled on the region’s public transit transfer discount, which utilizes SFMTA’s new tap-to-pay Clipper card system to offer discounted rides to passengers who use buses, light rail, and subway services.

“Shared mobility is a team effort, and Waymo’s autonomous ride-hailing service can help people to more easily access public transit networks while enhancing transportation ecosystems,” Adam Lenz, head of sustainability and environment at Waymo, said in a statement. “We’re excited to partner with local transit agencies and further bridge the transportation gap for commuters, tourists, and everyone in between through Waymo’s new transit rewards program.”

Some transportation experts worry that autonomous vehicles will siphon riders from buses and trains, which could eventually lead to service cuts. Most ridesharing customers don’t like transfering to another mode of transportation — they just want to get to their destination. And regular transit users, which tend to be more low-income, have difficulty affording many rideshare trips. Advocates also note that autonomous vehicles often position themselves as solutions to traffic congestion while also directly contributing to it.

Waymo is sensitive to criticism that it’s not a true friend to transit. It cites surveys that show over 50 percent of its customers in its top cities also use transit as evidence that it can play nicely with subways and buses.

In that vein, the company also announced dozens of dedicated robotaxi staging spaces at Caltrain stations, which the company says will help reduce wait times for commuters traveling to and from train stations. Waymo says it intends to expand both programs — discounts and dedicated staging spots — to more cities over time.

title: Corridor raises $25M seed to build a health benefits brokerage for SMBs
snippet: Corridor focuses on SMBs, which it says traditional brokerages often overlook because small accounts generate lower commissions than larger accounts.
fullText:
It’s been a while since Jackson Wagner left his job as a product lead at Scale AI in July 2022. Now, he’s building in a new space altogether: The new effort is an AI health benefits brokerage called Corridor that focuses on small businesses, which it says traditional brokerages often overlook because small accounts generate lower commissions even though they take the same amount of time as larger accounts. 

Corridor is betting an AI solution may help on that front. On its platform, customers work with human advisors while AI agents do administrative tasks in the background. The company says its agents can handle tedious office work like checking whether a doctor is in a customer’s insurance network, scheduling care, or providing a doctor updated health insurance information.

“We are every single employee and management’s concierge for all things healthcare,” Nikhil Aggarwal, the company’s CEO, told TechCrunch. 

On Monday, Corridor said it had raised a $25 million seed round led by Bain Capital Ventures. 

Corridor came about after Wagner was in a running accident, and the poor handling of his care led him down a path of “significant, consistent, chronic pain.”

“I developed a long list of complications that needed to be worked through one by one,” he said. 

He eventually left Scale AI to get a master’s degree in computer science and electrical engineering at UC Berkeley, before joining Build Robotics in 2023. Later, he teamed up with former Scale AI colleague Eric Qian to work on Capernaum AI, a startup building a clinical agent targeting musculoskeletal care and chronic pain. 

The two eventually approached Cold Start to see if they would fund Capernaum, but Aggarwal, who was a partner at Cold Start along with Jason Dong, saw a much larger opportunity. So the four of them took off and launched Corridor together. 

“Since health plans are the window through which the vast majority of Americans access healthcare, it became overwhelmingly clear that one of the highest impact things I could do to improve outcomes for individuals was to create a way for them to access better health plans,” Wagner said.

Other companies in this space include Ignition Benefits and Nava Benefits. 

Investors in Corridor’s round include BoxGroup, as well as executives from OpenAI, Scale AI, and Ramp. The startup is now preparing for Q4, since “80% of small businesses choose their health plan in Q4,” Aggarwal said.  

“Our vision is to build the most trusted healthcare institution in America,” he said. “To earn that, we are laser-focused on a simple promise: doing what we say we’re going to do for the businesses and employees we serve.”

title: iPhone users running iOS 27 can no longer downgrade to iOS 26
snippet: Apple today stopped signing iOS 26.6.2, which means iPhone users can no longer downgrade to non-iOS 27 system versions. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Apple today stopped signing iOS 26.6.2, which means iPhone users can no longer downgrade to non-iOS 27 system versions. Here’s why.

Apple no longer signing iOS 26.6.2 installs

When a user tries to install a version of iOS on their iPhone, part of the process involves checking with Apple’s servers to make sure that version is still authorized for installation. This is what’s referred to as signing, and it works for both upgrading or downgrading to any iOS version.

Because iOS updates often patch known security vulnerabilities, Apple keeps a rather short list of signed iOS versions. This prevents users from installing or downgrading to older versions that may contain flaws that could be exploited by attackers.

Today, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple stopped signing iOS 26.6.2. This means that users running iOS 27 can no longer downgrade to iOS 26.6.2, essentially closing the window on official downgrades to iOS 26.

Apple is no longer signing iOS 26.6.2, this means you can't downgrade to iOS 26 anymore from iOS 27

— Aaron (@aaronp613) September 21, 2026

It is worth noting that although Apple released iOS 26.7 last week, the company currently doesn’t officially offer a restore image for it, unlike iPadOS 26.7.

In practice, this means that iPhone users who are still running an earlier version of iOS 26 can install iOS 26.7 as an over-the-air update, but those already on iOS 27 cannot officially use it to downgrade.

fullText:
Following WhatsApp’s initial limited rollout of emoji reactions on the Apple Watch, the app is now rolling out support for the full set of emojis available on watchOS. Here are the details.

WhatsApp expands watchOS emoji reactions

Late last year, WhatsApp launched a full-featured Apple Watch app, with support for call notifications, voice messages, chat history, and emoji reactions.

The launch was largely good news for Apple Watch users, especially since WhatsApp’s presence on watchOS had previously been very limited, relying almost entirely on system notifications to read and reply to messages.

Still, emoji reactions came with one notable limitation: users could only choose from six preset emojis. Reacting with anything else required reaching for an iPhone.

Now, as reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is rolling out support for the full set of emojis available on watchOS. The site notes that tapping and holding a message still reveals the six default reactions, but users can now open a larger picker with recently used options and the full system emoji library split into categories.

Image: WABetaInfo

WhatsApp organizes emojis into 8 categories: Smileys, Nature, Food, Activity, Travel, Objects, Symbols, and Flags. Users can scroll through these to find the emoji they want to use as a reaction. They can tap any emoji category to expand the list. It is also possible to choose a recent emoji from the top of the list.

The site notes that although the feature is now officially rolling out, it may still take a few weeks to reach everyone, as WhatsApp is known for its gradual rollouts.

title: Meta’s Muse is outpacing ChatGPT’s early mobile launch
snippet: Meta’s new AI agent Muse has racked up more downloads and daily active users in the U.S. and Canada than ChatGPT did over the same period after its mobile debut, according to new estimates from Appfigures.
fullText:
Meta’s latest AI app, Muse, could be the social giant’s next major hit, new data suggests. According to just- released estimates from market intelligence provider Apptopia, Muse’s app on mobile devices has been downloaded more times during its first 12 days on the market than ChatGPT was in the 12 days after its debut. (This data compares the U.S. and Canada markets only.)

 Muse also has more daily active users than ChatGPT had at the time, the firm found.

Until now, it had been difficult to make an exact apples-to-apples comparison between these two apps, given that they had pursued different launch strategies. When ChatGPT arrived on mobile, it was made available globally, but only on iOS. Muse, meanwhile, is available across both Apple’s App Store and Google Play, but only in the U.S. and Canada.

To better align the numbers for comparison, Apptopia looked only at the iOS data for the U.S. and Canada for both apps during the first 12 days of their respective launches. In this subset of the data, Muse has now seen 1.8 million downloads to ChatGPT’s 1.3 million.

Overall, Muse has seen 2.8 million total installs globally in its first 12 days, the firm also said. Its growth hasn’t yet stagnated, either; Muse has moved up from its original position as No. 2 overall on the U.S. App Store immediately after its launch to now No. 1, as Business Insider reported on Friday. That jump put the app higher than ChatGPT, the outlet noted. Another firm, Appfigures, said at the time that Muse had then crossed 1 million downloads.

Image Credits:Appfigures

In addition, Apptopia’s data indicates that Muse’s U.S. daily active users are now higher than they were for ChatGPT at the same point after its launch. When comparing just the U.S. mobile app daily active users, Muse comes in higher with 642,000 daily users compared with 231,000 for ChatGPT at the time.

To be fair to the fact that Muse is available across both iOS and Android, while ChatGPT launched on iOS only, Apptopia narrowed the comparison to iOS alone. Yet, even here, Muse is coming in higher, with 359,000 daily active users on iOS, still above ChatGPT’s figures from that time period.

Apptopia can only provide third-party estimates about an app’s downloads and active users; it doesn’t have direct access to Meta’s internal figures. But even if these numbers are only correct from a general “ballpark” perspective, they indicate that Muse could have a shot at becoming Meta’s newest top app.

Meta already perfected its cross-promotion strategy when it launched Instagram’s Threads, which now has 500+ million users, thanks to heavy marketing and integrations in Meta’s largest apps, including Instagram and Facebook. Muse is likely to get a similar push, given that the AI app can connect with both of those platforms. It also works inside WhatsApp, so that could give it another boost. 

While Apptopia doesn’t have visibility into Meta’s cross-promotion efforts or ads directly, it did note that over 95% of Muse’s users are also Facebook users and 63% are Instagram users.

Meta, which has been asked for comment, has not yet shared public figures related to Muse’s early adoption.

snippet: Home security is going in all-new directions this year. I tested Abode’s sensors for gates, garages and more in my home.
fullText:
Abode's new sensors are a winning combo. / Tyler Lacoma/CNET Art

A new crop of security sensors has hit the shelves in 2026, and I like what I’ve tested. Tiny sensors that can detect tampering, tilting, movement and so on are offering all-new ways to watch over specific parts of our home. Abode is the first security kit company I’ve seen embrace this tech by offering its first entirely new sensors in years, made for parts of the home that security systems don’t usually watch.

Abode has two new products available now, a sensor made to monitor garage door access ($35), and an outdoor access sensor ($50) designed for gates, sheds, barns and any door open to the elements. I got to try them both around my home, and found them particularly effective and easy to set up compared to many of the sensors I’ve tested.

If you’ve been looking for a special device to help monitor access to backyards, detached buildings on your property, or garage doors that always seem to get left open, these sensors are a remarkable answer, particularly if you already have an Abode system. If not, I’ll cover what you need to know from my testing.

Unboxing and setup

Abode’s new sensors work flawlessly with its existing hub.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

I was able to fully test an Abode starter security kit as well as its two new sensors for this review, providing a clear look at how the security brand functions. As far as setup experiences go, this has been one of my speediest. And I’ve tested many different systems.

Abode’s beginner’s kit is small, offering an indoor sensor, motion sensor and fob, along with the hub. I was pleased to find out, after downloading the app and connecting the hub, the other base devices automatically added themselves and made the setup process effortless, smoother than nearly any other security system except possibly Ikea’s affordable sensors.

Adding the new garage and outdoor sensors also proved quick, with pairing happening only seconds after I installed the batteries and typed in the activation code.

Abode’s hub connects to new sensors in a snap.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

The one problem I have with Abode’s system is how the standard hub connects to Wi-Fi. This hub requires an Ethernet connection to your router or gateway, not only during setup but all the time. That’s a not-so-small problem if, like me, you have a router, gateway and other necessary devices already taking up all nearby outlets, which forced me to jury-rig a solution for the hub while I was testing.

Abode’s Iota hub does offer Wi-Fi, but that requires a more expensive upgrade to a $200 starter kit, not including extra sensors. It’s baffling that Abode’s standard hub still doesn’t support Wi-Fi when every other brand does. Check the outlets near your router before you choose this solution.

Garage sensor installation and performance

Abode’s garage sensor can sense any kind of tilt up and down.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Equipped with internal gyroscope technology, Abode’s garage door sensor is made to detect orientation, and setup couldn’t be simpler. Using the included adhesive strips, I slapped the small monitor on my closed garage door, and it began accurately detecting open/closed states immediately in the Abode app.

Smart garage door motors and controllers can also do something like this, plus app controls, but this is one of the first standard home security systems to expand to the garage, and adding a single $50 sensor is far more affordable than replacing your garage controller entirely. Abode let me know if the garage was left open, and advised me on unexpected garage door movement when no one was at home, just as advertised.

Placing the sensor shouldn’t be any trouble, no matter what kind of garage you have. It sticks onto the inside of the garage door where there is plenty of space, and doesn’t require any complicated calibration. You may have to reset the sensor after placement to make sure it’s reading open and closed states correctly, but that, too, takes only moments.

Finally, you could use this sensor on anything that tilts up and down like a garage door, such as tilting windows, so it could have other applications in your home.

Gate sensor installation and performance

Abode’s outdoor sensor is a little annoying to put together, but works like a charm.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Abode’s outdoor access sensor proved more complicated than the garage monitor. Bulkier than most access sensors and equipped with weather-resistance capabilities, it’s made to tell when anything outdoors opens and shuts. The two parts sense when they are close or when they’ve moved apart, with a bit of extra leeway compared to indoor sensors, since outdoor fences and other access zones have varied designs and gaps.

The complex housing proved adequate, but was more frustrating to install and is in need of some future refinements. The screw-in backplate, for example, had pop-out sections to make room for the screws, but the plastic base was so thick I couldn’t put out the sections at all, not even with a hammer that nearly destroyed the base itself (I used another tool to carve them out eventually, not an ideal situation). And the battery casing was so tight and awkwardly designed, I was afraid forcing the batteries in would harm the nearby, unprotected circuitry.

In these ways, the design feels a little too close to a prototype model for me, and it probably needs another pass or two. But it works, and works very well, when it’s finally set up.

Connected to my old fence gate, the sensor accurately and immediately told me whenever it was opened or closed. I’ve found that gate left open more than a few times, so this gave me welcome peace of mind. I also tested it during a stormy downpour, which did nothing to affect the performance of the sensor.

You may want to turn off beeps from the hub that sound every time it alerts to the sensor being opened, but Abode provided a setting to do just that. However, alerts and monitoring aren’t the only things these sensors can do.

App automations that benefit from Abode’s support

Abode’s app allows for customizations and automations, too.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

One of the most impressive parts of Abode’s security platform is how it maintains connections to other third-party smart home gadgets, from Google Home connections to the rare-to-find Apple support for certain devices. There are also Abode’s own devices, including cameras and smart locks, which naturally work with the system

Abode’s CUE function offers automations similar to Google Home or Apple Home.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

When Abode’s system is armed, triggering one of these garage or gate sensors can trip the system and sound a siren. But using the CUE automation tool in the Abode app, I found you can also set up many other types of automations, depending on what you want to activate.

This can include setting lights to turn on a warning glow if a fence gate is left open, or automatically unlocking your door when the garage is opened. You can also set times for these triggers to work, so they only function in the evening, on weekdays or only trigger after a certain time (the gate has been left open for 2 hours, for example). This adds more possibilities if you want to expand your smart home, but it’s not necessary to get value out of these sensors.

Remember, Abode’s app can also support third-party integrations with other devices.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

If you want to pay for an Abode subscription, you can add more features with plans starting at $80 a year, but these are mostly camera-focused, and I don’t think they’re necessary for these sensors at all.

Final thoughts on Abode’s new access sensors

Abode’s sensors signal helpful new trends in the home security world.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Abode’s newest sensors offer exceptional performance in spots other sensors aren’t really made for. They’re also more expensive than typical sensors, and the outdoor sensor might need another design pass in the future, but I otherwise found them easy to set up and start using for customized, helpful alerts.

One word of caution: Abode’s standard hub requires an Ethernet connection, so consider where you’ll put it, and if you’ll need to run Ethernet cable anywhere during installation. Otherwise, this system sets itself up in minutes.

I’m enjoying this 2026 wave of security tech innovations. They’re finding new applications in the home – and finding them with success. Aqara’s multipurpose sensor is one such model. Abode’s proved another strong example, so if you’ve been looking for extended security capabilities outdoors or in the garage, take note of this update.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

With degrees in Business Management, Literature and Technical Writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading, or gaming with good friends.

title: What do you actually use a laptop for, and would Googlebook be able to do it? [Poll]
snippet: Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced. more…
fullText:
Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced.

Our initial coverage of Googlebook is live, with Abner, Jordan, and Damien all walking away with a good first impression of Google’s efforts.

Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]

Yet, I’m unconvinced thus far. I’ve yet to get my hands on a Googlebook and, as someone sitting mostly in the same boat as you, our readers, I’m yet to be sold on this new platform. I simply don’t understand why it exists, even more so why Google seems to think it will succeed.

Google’s entire pitch around why you should buy a Googlebook more or less boils down to smartphone integration – specifically Android integration. Googlebook takes existing tools from ChromeOS and supercharges them, giving you the ability to mirror apps, sync files, and do a whole lot more between your Android phone and your laptop. And it does sound pretty good! As someone who currently juggles a MacBook with various Android phones, there are integrations I wish existed; instant hotspot and proper Quick Share support (AirDrop works, but tends to be wildly slow) are at the top of that list. 

	

Googlebook is delivering the MacBook + iPhone experience, just for Android users. That’s the pitch.

Where it falls flat for me is in the apparent functionality. At its core, Googlebook is Android, just with a desktop experience built on top. The core stuff is there – desktop-class Chrome browser, customizable desktop, keyboard shorts, the lot. But the app ecosystem is built around Android apps, web apps, and Linux apps. The same core as ChromeOS, just with a different priority and with better performance on the Android app side, as Abner and Damien both noticed.

That’s where I’m struggling to get on board.

There’s plenty you can do on a Googlebook, sure, just like there was plenty you could do on a Chromebook. But you’re still making a trade-off. Google pointed out that around 70% of things people do on a laptop are done through their browser (Chrome, of course). And, yeah, I’d say that’s about how much I do in the browser on my Windows desktop or my MacBook. That other 30%, though, is the “make or break” that eventually broke me on ChromeOS. For me, it largely came down to Adobe’s apps which, as it stands, still aren’t replicated on Googlebook. On Google’s own website, the company touts a Googlebook’s ability to use Photoshop and Lightroom, but that’s just with the mobile apps – not the full-featured apps you can use on you know, most other laptops. 

Google knows people use these apps; otherwise, it wouldn’t take up a place on this site in the first place – the same goes for games, where Google advertises tons of popular titles like Forza Horizon, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, and more, with only two of the games shown running natively and the rest delivered via GeForce Now.

The market has pretty clearly spoken in this regard. Chromebooks are out. There are remarkably few consumer-focused Chromebooks on the market today and, especially on the high end, it seems like hardly anyone is buying them – Google itself gave up on first-party Chromebooks over five years ago. 

To me at least, the reasoning seems obvious. When Chromebooks hit their stride, the market was full of compromises everywhere. There was no one perfect answer. But that’s changed in recent years. Apple’s M-series chips ushered in a new era for the MacBook which, in turn, influenced some major improvements across Windows laptops. Fast forward to today and there’s no lack of powerful, battery-efficient, thin & light laptop options and, despite “RAMageddon” ruining the price side of things, there’s been a huge push for more affordable machines in the wave of MacBook Neo and its clones – and those are very popular too. Giving up access to a full collection of full-featured apps for a lightweight operating system that gets roughly the same battery life for roughly the same price is a no-brainer, which means that Chromebooks are relegated to a niche. In enterprise/schools, for more affordable machines, for low-end hardware, ChromeOS still makes a lot of sense, but it’s a tough sell basically anywhere else, so you might be able to see why I’m so confused by Googlebook.

Googlebook’s pitch, again, isn’t bad, but does it make sense in today’s market? Who’s buying a laptop that’s inherently (and inarguably) restricted in what it can do, especially at a time when laptops are wildly inflated in price in the first place due to component shortages? 

This is the part where I turn the floor over to you.

Do you think Googlebook has stuck the landing? Has Google’s pitch resonated with you? 

	

Even more so, what are you using a laptop for in the first place? That’s perhaps the most important question around this. As mentioned, I’m personally using my laptop mostly in Chrome, with non-Chrome apps including the likes of Photoshop/Lightroom/Premiere, Spotify, Slack, and a handful of assorted other tools. There are a few of those I can replace – Spotify’s tablet interface should be a treat on a laptop, though I think Slack will be awful given how the Android app lacks any semblance of big-screen optimizations (on Android, as they’re immediately giving Apple something better), so maybe the Linux app will be better.

That’s just me. There are infinite ways people use their laptop. So, looking at what you do today, do you think a Googlebook can do it all? Vote in the poll below, then leave a comment.

title: SwiftKey ‘AI voice’ is Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text for other Android phones, works offline
snippet: Rambler in Gboard is perhaps one of the best Pixel 11 features, delivering powerful voice-to-text backed up by AI models. Once you’ve used it, it’s hard to switch back to anything else, but the Microsoft-owned SwiftKey is testing out a new “AI voice” feature that brings the core functionality of Pixel 11’s Rambler to basically any other Android phone. more…
fullText:
Rambler in Gboard is perhaps one of the best Pixel 11 features, delivering powerful voice-to-text backed up by AI models. Once you’ve used it, it’s hard to switch back to anything else, but the Microsoft-owned SwiftKey is testing out a new “AI voice” feature that brings the core functionality of Pixel 11’s Rambler to basically any other Android phone.

Available in the latest SwiftKey for Android beta release (v9.13.16.4), “AI voice” is an enhanced voice-to-text feature that allows you to speak and then let the AI step in to clean up filler words, format text, and more. In other words, it’s Pixel 11 Rambler, just without the exclusivity.

You tap a microphone icon to get started, with no live preview showing (the one thing we don’t love about Rambler) and a checkmark button ending the session, leaving the AI to process the result. 

Android Central notes that you’ll need to download an offline language model for “AI voice” to work, which is one big difference – it works offline, no servers required. The publication says that testing the feature on a Fold 8 required only 163MB of storage and worked with the device fully offline, something you can’t do with Rambler on the Pixel 11 series. Droid-Life also tested it out, finding that you can’t use voice commands to edit the test as Rambler allows, but it gets the job done.

	

While it initially seemed like Rambler might not be a Pixel exclusive, that’s where we’re at right now, so “AI voice” in SwiftKey is probably a good alternative for many. Wispr Flow is also available, as we previously covered, though its lack of keyboard integration can be a bit annoying at times.

You can download the SwiftKey for Android beta through the Play Store.

title: Kairos Power gets up to $100M from Samsung group to build nuclear reactor for Google
snippet: Future Google supplier Kairos Power inked a deal with Samsung C&T to help build its first 50-megawatt nuclear power plant.
fullText:
Kairos Power has picked engineering firm Samsung C&T to help build its 50-megawatt demonstration reactor for Google, which the nuclear startup is aiming to have completed by 2030.

As part of the deal, Samsung C&T will make an equity investment in Kairos and provide “in-kind” engineering services, the combination of which is worth up to $100 million, Kairos Power said Monday. The equity investment will make up $70 million of the total, a Kairos spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Samsung C&T has built or helped build about a dozen nuclear reactors around the globe.

Kairos is part of a wave of nuclear startups that have benefited from the surge in power demand from AI data centers. Google first signed a deal with the company in fall 2024, calling on Kairos to build nuclear reactors capable of generating about half a gigawatt of electricity by 2035. 

Currently, Kairos is building two reactors in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. The first, Hermes 1, is a low-power demonstrator that will help the company refine its commercial design. The second, Hermes 2, is Kairos’ first commercial-scale reactor. Output from Hermes will count as the first 50 megawatts of its deal with Google.

The startup received approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in late 2024 to build the reactors. It expects Hermes 2 to begin operating in 2030, in line with its original agreement with Google.

Hermes 2 will be a fluoride salt-cooled high-temperature reactor, a design that has been floated for years but never built at commercial scale. Fluoride salts have high boiling points, which will help keep pressure levels low. That, in turn, will limit the risk of high-pressure blowouts in case of any parts failures. 

Kairos is also using a relatively new form of nuclear fuel known as TRISO, which encapsulates tiny seeds of uranium fuel in layers of ceramic and carbon, which are then loaded into billiard ball-sized spheres. The arrangement is intended to prevent meltdowns.

The startup has about five years to get its first power plant up and running, which is an accelerated but manageable timeline in the nuclear industry. To fulfill the terms of its deal with Google, Kairos will need to move even faster on subsequent reactors, something Samsung C&T might be able to help with.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. 

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College.

title: iOS 27: My favorite new iPhone features (other than AI)
snippet: Apple released iOS 27 to everyone this week, and the headlining changes are Siri AI and the array of new Apple Intelligence features. However, the update also includes plenty of non-AI features. Here are a few of my favorite iOS 27 features (other than Siri and AI). more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27 to everyone this week, and the headlining changes are Siri AI and the array of new Apple Intelligence features. However, the update also includes plenty of non-AI features.

Here are a few of my favorite iOS 27 features (other than Siri and AI).

The new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are fantastic in iOS 27, but there are some others: 

In the Music app, Apple has updated AutoMix with new transitions. I was a big fan of the initial version of AutoMix that launched in iOS 26, and the new transitions in iOS 27 are noticeably better and more immersive.

In the Photos app, iCloud Shared Albums now offer full-resolution sharing. This is a big upgrade that makes it significantly easier to share photos and videos with others without compromising image quality.

You can now set an independent volume for alarms in the Clock app. This new option is in the Settings app under “Sounds & Haptics.” This means your alarms and timers no longer have to match your ringtone volume.

iOS 27 adds an all-new extra-large widget size for your Home Screen. There are full-screen widgets for apps like Music, Photos, Weather, and Calendar.

You can now swipe away the Now Playing widget from the Lock Screen in iOS 27. 

On the Lock Screen, you can now move the clock to the top widget row, so it no longer gets in the way of your wallpaper.

In the Photos app, you can now save a specific video frame as a photo. This means you no longer have to manually take a screenshot of a video you’ve already taken to get a specific frame as a separate photo.

The Apple Pay checkout flow has been significantly overhauled, making it a lot easier to switch between payment cards.

iOS 27 adds landscape support to more apps, which is great as someone who keeps their iPhone docked at their desk all day. This includes apps like Music, Reminders, Weather, and more.

The Find My app has a new design in iOS 27, plus more flexible sharing options. In particular, I like that the new design shows me more specific location information without having to tap on a specific person.

When you copy something to your iPhone’s clipboard in iOS 27, you’ll see a built-in paste shortcut above the keyboard the next text field you go to. This makes it a lot quicker to copy and paste text, links, photos, and more between apps.

In CarPlay, there’s now an audio scrubber that lets you skip to different parts of a song or podcast right on your car’s display.

What are your favorite non-AI features in iOS 27? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Oura’s $2.2B IPO is mostly a payday for existing shareholders
snippet: Forerunner Ventures plans to sell its entire stake in Oura for as much as $1.26 billion, according to Oura's latest IPO filing.
fullText:
Smart ring maker Oura is looking to raise as much as $2.2 billion in its upcoming IPO, but it looks like its current investors will be the ones making money in the process.

According to the company’s updated IPO filing, Oura and its shareholders are together offering 50 million shares at a price range of $40 to $44 each. But most of the IPO’s proceeds will go to shareholders, who are offering 36.5 million shares, or almost two-thirds of the total.

If the company lists at $42 per share, the midpoint of the price range, that would result in proceeds of about $1.53 billion for the shareholders and $567 million for the company, before fees and expenses.

The bulk of that will go to Forerunner Ventures, the company’s second-largest shareholder. The venture firm plans to sell its entire 9.3% stake of about 28.7 million shares for about $1.20 billion (assuming the shares list at $42) before underwriting fees and taxes. Forerunner’s shares account for nearly 80% of the shares being sold by existing shareholders in the deal.

Forerunner first invested in Oura in the company’s 2020 $28 million Series B round, according to PitchBook.

Meanwhile, Oura doesn’t look to be treating this IPO as a fundraising event. At the $42 midpoint, the company expects net proceeds of $532.6 million and plans to use about $526.4 million to pay off accumulated tax obligations related to employee share grants that will vest at the time of the IPO.

That would leave the company with roughly $6.2 million for general corporate purposes, according to the filing.

In a way, this is kind of a flex by Oura, which is essentially using this IPO to give its early backers an exit. It’s also fulfilling tax obligations without turning to debt, as companies sometimes do, or touching its cash, which sat at about $372 million at the end of June. 

The offering comes as Oura is growing quickly, with subscriptions becoming a larger source of revenue. The membership business is seemingly a very profitable endeavor for Oura, with an 89% gross margin. Membership revenue more than doubled to $240.5 million in the period, accounting for about 20% of the company’s sales. Hardware still made up most of the company’s revenue, at $974 million.

Oura now expects to finish the fiscal year ending September 30 with about 5.7 million paying members, which would nearly double the number from a year earlier.

Oura could end up with a market cap of $14.1 billion if it lists at the top of the proposed price range.

The company was valued at approximately $11 billion in October 2025, when it raised $900 million in a round that was led by Fidelity and saw participation from ICONIQ, Whale Rock, and Atreides. It had raised $200 million at a $5.2 billion valuation less than a year earlier. The company has raised about $2.06 billion to date, according to PitchBook.

Ram is a financial and tech reporter and editor. He covered North American and European M&A, equity, regulatory news and debt markets at Reuters and Acuris Global, and has also written about travel, tourism, entertainment and books.

title: Adobe Premiere for Android launches for free with layered video editing, YouTube templates
snippet: Months after it arrived on iPhone, Adobe Premiere’s mobile version is now available on Android devices with layered video editing, templates, foldable optimization, and more. more…
fullText:
Months after it arrived on iPhone, Adobe Premiere’s mobile version is now available on Android devices with layered video editing, templates, foldable optimization, and more.

Adobe Premiere Pro is widely recognized as a powerful video editing suite on desktop machines, but Adobe’s last version for mobile devices vanished a while back. Now, Adobe Premiere is once again available on Android, delivering what appears to be a very capable video editor that promises to be a solution across all Android devices.

This is the same app that debuted on iPhone in late 2025, and it brings quite a few features with it.

Some of the key features include:

	

Enhance Audio: Reduce background noise, clean up voiceovers, etc

Multi-track timeline: Manage multiple videos, sound effects, music, etc

Templates: Custom-made templates to speed up editing

Effects: Transitions, creative assets, Adobe Stock integration

Export: Up to 4K editing + export

The app already has wide support of different Android devices and form factors, including optimization for foldable smartphones. There’s also a built-in voice recorder.

Adobe says that more features are coming, including support for Adobe Fonts in creating text overlays, the ability to transfer projects to Premiere Pro on desktop, “beat detection,” cropping, and more. 

The big deal here, though, is that Adobe Premiere for Android is free. You don’t need a Creative Cloud subscription, you don’t need to sit through ads, and there are no watermarks either. Adobe says you can purchase upgrades for “additional generative credits and storage,” but that’s optional.

Requirements for Adobe Premiere on Android include 5GB of RAM or more and Android 13 or newer.

title: iOS 27 makes your iPhone faster in these 30+ ways
snippet: iOS 27 is now available to everyone, and one of the big changes is that it makes your iPhone a lot faster. In fact, Apple has outlined more than 30 ways in which your iPhone will be faster after you update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is now available to everyone, and one of the big changes is that it makes your iPhone a lot faster. In fact, Apple has outlined more than 30 ways in which your iPhone will be faster after you update.

How iOS 27 makes your iPhone faster

When Apple announced iOS 27 in June, the company emphasized that it combed through its software to make it faster and more reliable. “Improvements across platforms push key system capabilities forward so everyday tasks feel faster, smoother, and more enjoyable,” Apple said.

Here are more than 30 ways iOS 27 makes your iPhone faster:

Faster loading of new captures in Photos (up to 70% faster)

Faster to open full-screen view from Photos widget

Faster rendering of Collections tab in Photos

Faster to start uploading to iCloud Photos

Faster Camera launch in Low Power Mode

Faster to add recent camera captures in Messages

Faster start page content loading in Safari

Faster web application performance in Safari

Faster handling of JavaScript in Safari

Faster message loading in Mail

Faster HomeKit accessory pairing

Faster smart home accessory updates

Faster Now Playing view loading in Music

Faster Apple Music playback start

Faster board previews in Freeform

Faster data updates in the Health app

Faster workout start in the Workout app

Faster Lock Screen switching

Faster app launches (up to 30% faster)

Faster AirPlay connections to Apple TV and HomePod

Faster network file browsing

Faster and more reliable NFC reading

Faster Voice Control response in iOS

Faster entry and exit from Assistive Access and Guided Access modes

Faster PDF saving

Faster Text Recognition in photos and documents

Faster Rapid Return to Service

Faster loading of emoji and sticker keyboards

Faster shortcuts and actions indexing in Spotlight

Faster multilingual text processing for handwriting in multiple languages

Faster AirDrop transfers (up to 80% faster)

Faster AirDrop recipient discovery

Faster access to shared content on iCloud.com

9to5Mac’s Take

iOS 27 is compatible with iPhone models dating back to the iPhone 11. In fact, Apple even says that some of its performance metrics are based on testing it conducted with the iPhone 11 lineup.

For example, Apple says that apps launch up to 30% faster with iOS 27. This statistic is based on testing Apple performed on the iPhone 11 Pro Max, comparing app launch speeds between one model running iOS 26.4.2 and another running iOS 27.

All of this is very impressive — especially for people using “older” iPhone models. Apple has fixed enough bugs and made such a jump in performance that I think most iPhone users will notice a big improvement when they install iOS 27 later this year. It’s particularly impressive when you consider Apple made all these improvements to performance while simultaneously implementing a ground-up revamp of Siri.

title: It’s not just your class, Google Classroom is down in apparent outage
snippet: An influx of reports suggests that Google Classroom is suddenly out, while other Workspace apps seem unaffected. more…
fullText:
An influx of reports suggests that Google Classroom is suddenly out, while other Workspace apps seem unaffected.

Google Classroom appears to be out, according to a sudden outage spike on Downdetector starting at 12:33 PM ET. In a little under an hour, reports jumped from a clean zero to over 500, indicating the issue is widespread, more than localized to a few disconnections.

The Google Classroom program is still being utilized and improved on, even after the COVID-19 crisis forced students to learn from their own homes. Google has recently begun integrating third-party add-ons to make the web app more useful for those who still make use of the digital learning aid.

It doesn’t appear that any other Google Workspace apps are affected by the outage, other than Classroom. It isn’t uncommon for multiple Google Workspace apps to experience an outage at the same time. title: Apple pushes UK court to lift secrecy around encryption backdoor order
snippet: In a hearing today, Apple challenged the UK government’s refusal to publicly confirm whether it has issued an order requiring the company to provide access to encrypted user data. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a hearing today, Apple challenged the UK government’s refusal to publicly confirm whether it has issued an order requiring the company to provide access to encrypted user data. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Early last year, The Washington Post reported that the British government had secretly ordered Apple to create a security backdoor into all iCloud content uploaded by users worldwide.

The order itself was also subject to strict secrecy rules, preventing even Apple from publicly confirming or discussing the demand.

The British government has maintained a policy of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual orders of this kind, while companies subject to them are also restricted from disclosing that they have received one.

As a result of the reported but officially unconfirmed order, Apple removed the option to enable Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for iCloud users in the UK.

That’s because with ADP enabled, iCloud Backup and other additional categories of iCloud data are end-to-end encrypted. So instead of complying with the UK’s backdoor order, Apple stopped offering ADP to new users in the UK altogether, even though the original order reportedly applied to users worldwide.

At this point, Apple’s fight with the UK government was two-pronged: it was challenging both the underlying demand for access to encrypted data and the secrecy rules preventing it from publicly discussing that demand.

In April, 2025, judges rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep even the basic details of Apple’s legal challenge secret, ruling that disclosing the existence of the case would not harm national security.

A few months after that, the British government gave up on requiring data from American users as part of the secret mandate, as a result of pressure from the White House. The demand did not disappear entirely, however: Britain later issued a new notice targeting Apple users in the UK.

Fast-forward to a few weeks ago, when it emerged that Apple had launched a second legal challenge against the UK government after the original worldwide order was replaced by a new one specifically targeting British users.

Which brings us to today.

Apple challenges mandate secrecy

As reported by Reuters, Apple today challenged the UK government’s continued refusal to confirm or deny the existence of the new Technical Capability Notice during a hearing before the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) in London.

According to Reuters, Apple’s lawyer argued that the government’s secrecy policy prevents meaningful public discussion of the case, and undermines the principle of open justice.

From the report:

At Thursday’s hearing at the IPT, Ben ​Jaffey, the lawyer for campaign groups, Privacy International and Liberty, said the government’s position had “become farcical”.

“The horse has long bolted,” he noted, ‌meaning ⁠it was already public knowledge.

U.S. politicians and officials had publicly referred to the original notice while unnamed UK government sources had also confirmed it to the press, he said.

Both he and Apple’s lawyer said that the UK government’s NCND policy was an affront to open justice and prevented meaningful public discussion of the issue.

To be clear, today’s hearing focused on the secrecy surrounding the order, not on whether the UK government was legally entitled to demand access to Apple’s encrypted data in the first place.

Following today’s hearing, the IPT will now decide whether the government can continue relying on its “neither confirm nor deny” policy in this case. Reuters says a full hearing on Apple’s challenge to the underlying Technical Capability Notice is unlikely before next year.

title: Apple challenges OpenAI’s forensic analysis in trade secrets case, seeks access to hardware R&D
snippet: Apple has asked the court overseeing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to let its own experts review forensic images used in the case, while also seeking documents related to parts of OpenAI’s hardware R&D. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has asked the court overseeing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to let its own experts review forensic images used in the case, while also seeking documents related to parts of OpenAI’s hardware R&D. Here are the details.

A bit of background

In early July, Apple sued former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, accusing them of trade secret misappropriation.

The lawsuit involves former Apple employees who allegedly took confidential information with them when they left the company. Apple also alleges that former employee Chang Liu coached another Apple employee on materials to review ahead of an OpenAI interview, while Tang Tan directed Apple job candidates to bring hardware components and other materials to interviews.

More recently, Apple said an initial forensic inspection of a MacBook used by Liu after leaving the company showed that he had used a confidential Apple circuit schematic to run a simulation while working at OpenAI. Apple also said the MacBook pointed to Liu’s use of a Mac mini, which the company has since sought access to as part of the case.

OpenAI has since refuted Apple’s allegations, arguing that this situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making,” since the company’s allegedly lax offboarding and security practices made it easier for employees to unintentionally retain access to confidential information after leaving.

One of the many points of contention in the case is Apple’s request for expedited discovery, which OpenAI has opposed. Another is Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction that would restrict OpenAI’s use of Apple’s alleged trade secrets while the lawsuit proceeds, potentially affecting its ongoing hardware development.

Apple argues that it needs expedited access to certain evidence precisely because OpenAI is still developing its hardware product, meaning that any alleged use of Apple’s trade secrets could become further intertwined with that work and increasingly difficult to undo.

OpenAI, in turn, argues that Apple has not shown why a separate expedited discovery process is warranted, and says that Apple’s requests are too broad.

Due to this impasse, the court asked both sides to submit a joint filing laying out their respective positions on expedited discovery. That document, filed last Friday, has now been made public.

Apple wants access to forensic images, R&D material

In the joint filing, Apple asks the court to allow its own forensic experts to review the underlying forensic images that the defendants’ experts relied on to analyze Liu’s devices and determine whether he accessed or used Apple’s confidential information after leaving the company.

Apple says one of its forensic experts has already identified what it describes as “critical flaws” in that analysis, and argues that its experts need direct access to determine whether there were other problems with the defendants’ forensic analysis.

Here’s Apple:

Apple’s forensic expert has already uncovered several critical flaws in the analysis conducted by Defendants’ experts, including (1) failures to locate files on Mr. Liu’s Mac Mini that were demonstrably used and stored on that device and (2) incorrect conclusions that the presence of files with zero bytes or an empty kMDItemLastUsedDate field on the Mac Mini means those files were not accessed. […] Giving Apple’s experts direct access to these forensic images is critical to understanding what other errors Defendants’ experts may have committed.

OpenAI argues that Apple’s experts should not be given unrestricted access to the forensic images, proposing instead that a neutral forensic expert handle them under a jointly agreed protocol.

Apple argues that this would put it at a disadvantage, since the defendants’ own forensic experts have already had direct access to the same material.

In addition to the forensic material, Apple is seeking expedited access to documents related to OpenAI’s hardware development, including work on metal finishes, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI previously argued that its metal finishes were developed independently, without using Apple confidential information, and that a simulation Liu ran using an Apple confidential file had nothing to do with its upcoming product.

Apple is now asking for the underlying development records so it can test those claims, which OpenAI says is just an attempt to “snoop on a competitor.”

Here’s Apple:

As Defendants have now put their development at issue, they must prove their assertions that they “developed their own standard metal finishes and colors” by producing supporting documents. Apple is not requesting “a complete technical record of OpenAI’s development of any technology,” as OpenAI asserts, but rather technology related to “metal finishes, power management, or battery functionality,” the technology that Defendants have put at issue in defending against Apple’s claims.

And here’s OpenAI:

This demand for a complete technical record of OpenAI’s development of any technology within Apple’s broad categories is overbroad and premature, and an apparent attempt to snoop on a competitor. Apple’s request is not even limited to OpenAI’s first product under development, which Apple expressed ostensible concern about […]—it encompasses any research and development. And it requires OpenAI to reveal its trade secrets before Apple has revealed its own (which are the subject of this lawsuit)—placing this request far beyond the scope of merits-based discovery, let alone “expedited” discovery.

The joint filing also touches on several other points of contention, including:

Apple’s broader request for forensic images from devices used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting “Alyssa” Peng, and another OpenAI employee that contain or previously contained what Apple defines as “Apple Originated Information;

Records related to Liu’s use of AI tools, after the defendants said a forensic investigation found no evidence that he used an Apple confidential file with platforms including ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;

Interview-related documents from OpenAI’s Consumer Hardware Products Group, including materials showing what the group actually uses during interviews and communications with departing Apple employees;

Interrogatories that OpenAI says could reach more than 400 former Apple employees now working at the company.

Apple is also seeking the full LINE conversations between Liu and Peng, which include exchanges in which Peng asked Liu technical questions about Apple work after he had left the company.

The defendants had already submitted excerpts from those conversations in opposing Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction, but Apple argues that it should be allowed to review the full exchanges rather than only the messages the defendants chose to submit.

title: iOS 27 adds convenient new iPhone feature you’ll use all the time
snippet: iOS 27 has arrived, with Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features as big highlights. But one of my favorite features is a convenient addition for quickly pasting items from your iPhone’s clipboard. Here’s how it works. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has arrived, with Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features as big highlights. But one of my favorite features is a convenient addition for quickly pasting items from your iPhone’s clipboard. Here’s how it works.

iOS 27 adds paste shortcut above keyboard for one-tap access to your clipboard

Every year Apple adds a bunch of new features to iOS, and this year that includes upgrades to Apple Wallet, Messages, CarPlay, and more.

Many new features might go easily overlooked by the average iPhone user.

But there’s one iOS 27 addition in particular that I suspect readers will find themselves using a lot.

After you copy text to your iPhone’s clipboard, or a link or photo, iOS 27 adds a paste shortcut above the keyboard when you open a new text field.

The idea is simple: if you copy something, then immediately switch to another app, or open some other text field, Apple knows there’s a very good chance you want to paste there.

So rather than requiring you to open the copy/paste menu and hit paste from there, the paste suggestion appears automatically above the keyboard—offering one-tap convenience.

You’ll even see a preview of what’s on the clipboard, right there in the top keyboard row. So if it’s text, you’ll know what that text is, and if it’s an image you’ll see a small thumbnail preview.

It’s the kind of feature that I never would have thought to ask for, but in using the iOS 27 beta over the summer it quickly proved very convenient in everyday use.

title: Everyone can find a reason to dislike data center construction
snippet: Inside two years of fraught AI data center debates in Pennsylvania.
fullText:
Frontier AI labs are convinced that scaling up computation is the path to improving artificial intelligence, and they’ve put their money where their mouths are, to the tune of trillions of dollars of planned data center projects.

The rest of us? Surveys of public opinion say that more than 60% of Americans favor limiting new data centers, particularly in their communities. And the longest-running surveys show that sentiment is growing fast. Data center projects worth $68 billion were disrupted by local opponents in the second quarter of 2026, according to the trackers at Data Center Watch. 

AI companies and their investors have a hard time reconciling the growing demand for their products with opposition to the key infrastructure behind it. Some answers from the industry, like the idea that data center opposition is a product of secretive Chinese meddling, don’t really pass the smell test.

Today, a new report from the nonprofit Data & Society offers a deeper look at what is activating opposition to data centers. It is the result of 18 months of ethnographic fieldwork by a team of researchers who interviewed 44 Pennsylvanians between 2024 and 2026. The authors, who are critical of the way AI has been pitched, aren’t trying to measure the empirical impact of data centers, but instead want to understand the way people experience the debate over their construction.

“One of the strengths of ethnography and doing research on the ground for an extended period of time is piercing the bubble of AI hype,” Livia Garofalo, a Data & Society researcher, told TechCrunch. “People are making sense of the dissonances between AI being the next inevitable industrial revolution, and fears about AI.”

When the authors began their work, data centers were being pitched as key to economic development. Governor Josh Shapiro headlined a July 2025 summit celebrating $90 billion in data center and AI infrastructure investment. A year later, Shapiro signed an order imposing new requirements on data center projects and removing them from a regulatory fast-track initiative. Someone read the writing on the wall.

The authors say the message from industry that AI is “inevitable” has landed poorly with Pennsylvania residents. They point to the state’s historic waves of industrialization, including coal mining, the early days of the oil industry, steel manufacturing, and fracking, experiences that have left residents suspicious of utopian industrial schemes.

“People in Pennsylvania especially have incredible experience with industrial change, have deep lineages of industrial trauma, enough to sniff when things don’t feel right to them,” Maia Woluchem, a program director at Data & Society who co-authored the report, said. 

Still, trade unions are perhaps the greatest source of support for data center projects, thanks to the potential jobs they represent. Even acknowledging that, once built, these data centers won’t be major sources of employment, unions see the projects as a lifeline to rebuild their ranks.

There’s an influence campaign, alright

In contrast to the industry’s fears of foreign influence, the researchers describe the work of AI boosters as a kind of propaganda campaign, pointing to the Data Center Coalition, a trade group that has set up websites like “Pennsylvania Connects” to boost projects and spent at least $19,000 lobbying the state government last year.

In spite of the boosterism, resistance has grown, and in unlikely ways. The researchers said they were surprised by the diversity of the opposition to these projects, calling it not bipartisan but post-partisan.

“We don’t want to romanticize that everyone is having this kumbaya moment, [but AI is] forcing people to be in conversation together about futures that they want and presents that they want … these fights are incredibly organic,” Woluchem said, pointing to a variety of sources of opposition: Sometimes it is simply folks who are against development — classic NIMBYs — but the coalition grows from there. There are people who dislike AI as a technology and the corporate interests behind it, environmental groups concerned about water usage and energy-related emissions, and those with more nebulous concerns about public health.

What’s striking, though, is how often material interests are top of mind. People are concerned that data center electrical usage will affect their own power bills, worried that data centers will drive down property values, or are upset by the playbook that data center builders use to get their way — tactics such as asking local officials to sign non-disclosure agreements.

“There is a significant group of people who are just really clued into their town hall meetings and might notice that wow, a representative from Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, showed up here, or a data center developer showed up at my community meeting …that’s a little odd,” Woluchem notes. “And my council person, who I have previously had a relationship with, now won’t talk to me about this sort of thing.”

It’s this patchwork quilt of motivations for anti-data center activism that presents such a challenge for the AI industry: There’s no simple way to alleviate this raft of concerns. The problem is trust, which has already deviled the industry.

“It is an intimate and relational trust that is now being inserted in people’s lives by these industries,” Garofalo said. “I’m alone in my house, and I’m talking to a chatbot, and I’m feeling loved and cared for, and yet I know that this is a commodity, and I know I’m being extracted upon.”

He has closely covered the rise of the private space industry and is the author of  Rocket Billionaires: Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and the New Space Race. Formerly, he was a senior reporter at Quartz, the global business news site, for more than a decade, and began his career as a political reporter in Washington, D.C.

title: The new Boox e-ink devices get Android 16 out of the box, including Palma 3
snippet: Boox just announced three new e-ink devices on Android 16; the largest tablet is available now, but you’ll have to wait a little longer for the updated Palma 3. more…
fullText:
Boox just announced three new e-ink devices on Android 16; the largest tablet is available now, but you’ll have to wait a little longer for the updated Palma 3.

E-ink devices have taken off in the last couple of years for a couple of reasons. The main reasoning that comes to mind is the natural disconnect that comes from using an e-ink device instead of a traditional modern OLED smartphone or tablet. Another likely has something to do with the universal appeal of an e-reader or note-taking device that lets you access apps from the Google Play Store.

Boox announced three new additions to its lineup of Android e-ink devices:

Boox Note Air6 C

Boox Note Mini C

Boox Palma 3

All three will run Android 16 out of the box, which is notable because the latest public version of Android is only one generation ahead of that. It wouldn’t have been a surprise if these devices were still a generation or two behind that. Two could be considered tablets, while the Palma is a generational upgrade to the company’s beloved compact e-reader that looks like an Android phone, at first glance.

	

The Note Air6 C is the only model Boox says is available starting today. It’s the workhorse of the three, with a new internal processor and a reasonable 3,700mAh battery. The new processor boosts the Note Air6 C’s performance with features like Dual Notes that let you annotate two documents in split-screen mode.

Boox mentions the large Android tablet also has new AI features for transcripts and document scanning. But the real improvement might just be an upgraded refresh rate that increases performance by up to 40%. Refresh rates have always been a sore point for e-ink tablets, but it’s always come with the territory for a paper-like display.

The 10.3-inch tablet has a color display that works with the included Pen3 stylus. It also wouldn’t be a Boox tablet without a front-light with temperature controls for any-time viewing.

The Note Mini C isn’t available to order just yet. It’s an 8.52-inch Android e-ink tablet aimed at users who need a little more portability from Boox devices. Similar to the Note Air6 C, it has a Kaleido 3 color e-ink display with a front light, as well as an octa-core processor. It has a little less battery power at 3,150mAh. On an e-ink tablet, that still goes a long way.

We’re also getting an upgraded model in the Palma series with the Palma 3. The form factor has grown more popular since Boox began teasing the Picco. The Palma 3 is slightly bigger and has a 6.13-inch display.

This version has a “refined anodized aluminum frame” instead of the plastic exterior seen on the previous models. The rear panel is made from fiberglass that has a “paper-textured” feel. Under that panel sits a 3,950mAh battery, which hasn’t changed from even the original Palma.

Boox hasn’t announced a release date for the Note Mini C or the Palma 3, but the Note Air6 C is available now. The Note Air6 C starts at $579. Boox’s Note Mini C is priced at $579, too, and the Palma 3 will be $339 at launch.

title: Samsung’s battery upgrades for Galaxy S27 Ultra and Pro leak – is it enough?
snippet: A new leak reveals the battery sizes of Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro including some long overdue upgrades, but do you think it’s enough? more…
fullText:
A new leak reveals the battery sizes of Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro including some long overdue upgrades, but do you think it’s enough?

Following Samsung’s adoption of silicon-carbon battery tech on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series, it was inevitable that the Galaxy S27 series would jump on board. That’s not directly confirmed yet, but a regulatory leak (via GSMArena) offers a look at the rated capacities of Samsung’s new flagships.

These are rated capacities, with advertised capacity generally being a bit higher. As a comparison, the Galaxy S26 Ultra has an advertised battery capacity of 4,855 mAh, but an advertised capacity of 5,000 mAh. So, with that in mind:

Galaxy S27 Ultra: Rated 5,534 mAh | Advertised likely 5,700~ mAh 

Galaxy S27 Pro: Rated 5,087 mAh | Advertised likely 5,200~ mAh 

There’s no direct comparison for the Pro model, but the Galaxy S26 sits at 4,300 mAh at around the same physical size, so this is a huge jump. 

	

For Samsung’s full-size flagship, the Galaxy S27 Ultra is looking at a jump of around 700 mAh. It’s only 14%, but that’s a considerable step up after years of stagnation. Both devices are also listed with 60W wired charging.

But, in a world where silicon-carbon batteries are pushing Android flagships upwards of 6,000, 7,000, and even bigger batteries. The Oppo Find X10, for example, is rumored to pack in an 8,000 mAh battery when it debuts later this month. 

What do you think? Did Samsung do enough? Sound off in the comments below.
