title: September 2026 Pixel Drop: VIPs widget redesign, more Pixel Watch gestures
snippet: Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Pixel Drop. This is a smaller update, with Android 17 QPR1 bringing the bulk of new features and changes. That said, recent weeks have seen updates for Pixel Journal, Now Playing, Recorder, Screenshots, and Weather. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Pixel Drop. This is a smaller update, with Android 17 QPR1 bringing the bulk of new features and changes. That said, recent weeks have seen updates for Pixel Journal, Now Playing, Recorder, Screenshots, and Weather.

Phones

Google has redesigned the Pixel VIPs widget to let you quickly call and text contacts with a single tap from your homescreen instead of having to first open the bottom sheet.

A new floating navigation overlay lets you swipe the bottom of your screen to switch between your favorite people. Finally, Pixel VIPs will show glanceable notification badges on the widget. 

This redesign is rolling out for the Pixel 6+ in all regions and languages with version 2.0 of the Pixel VIPs app/service and Google Contacts 4.77+.

	

After introducing on the Pixel 11 series, Pause Point is now coming to the Pixel 6 and newer. This Digital Wellbeing feature “adds a pause before you open a distracting app of your choice.”

Updated: Scam Detection warnings now appear in the Gboard suggestions strip “wherever you chat.” The “Likely scam” warning will appear ”when you start typing a response to a suspicious message.” Available on the Pixel 6+ in the US, processing happens on your device.

Additionally, the existing Scam Detection in notifications is expanding to nine new countries (Australia, Canada, France, Germany, India, Japan, Mexico, Singapore, and the United Kingdom), as well as six new languages (Arabic, French, German, Portuguese, Japanese, and Spanish).

To mark the release of Harry Potter: The Full-Cast Audio Editions, there are three new Pixel Themes. This covers wallpapers, icons, and sounds, with eligible Pixel users also getting a two-month Audible free trial.

Pixel Watch

Owners of the Pixel Watch 3 and 4 can now scroll through their notification tray using the one-handed pinch gesture. This has been quite convenient on the PW5.

Meanwhile, the Pixel Watch 4 receives an updated raise-to-talk model that improves accuracy and performance when activating Gemini.

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by CleanMyMac by MacPaw. With the release of macOS 27 Golden Gate, use CleanMyMac first to free up space, optimize your system, and ensure your new Mac runs at 100% on day one. Learn more.

macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t give the Photos app a dramatic redesign. Instead, Photos gains a surprisingly broad set of various improvements this year. These range from Apple Intelligence-powered editing, new ways to organize and sort your collection, better sharing tools, and much more.

More powerful Apple Intelligence editing

The flashiest updates to the Photos app in macOS 27 Golden Gate live in a new Tools pane. They require Apple Intelligence on a compatible Mac.

Clean Up gets a significant quality boost. Apple says it can now handle larger objects and more complex scenes with more realistic results.

Separately, a fast mode is intended for small blemishes, while high quality mode tackles more intricate edits not possible before.

The new Extend tool uses generative models to expand an image beyond its original edges.

That can help when straightening a horizon, changing an aspect ratio, or simply creating more space around a subject. Extend is also available from the Crop tool.

Then there’s Spatial Reframing.

First, Photos builds a 3D view of a scene using on-device spatial models. This lets you rotate around a subject, pan, or zoom to change the apparent camera position.

When the new perspective exposes gaps, image models generate the missing areas.

In macOS 27, iCloud Shared Albums finally support full-resolution sharing and all common photo and video formats.

They’re also becoming much friendlier to people outside the Apple ecosystem. Friends using Android or Windows can join a Shared Album and contribute their own photos through iCloud.com.

Apple is also addressing some everyday friction. You can save every photo from a Shared Album to your personal library with a single click.

For albums that do not need to live forever, there is a new option to have them expire after 30 days.

Slideshows, ratings, and a new collection

Next, Photos is bringing back more control over slideshows. You can turn any selection of photos and videos into a slideshow, then customize its slide duration, transition style, and music.

After that, the finished slideshow can be saved as a video file in your photo library. That makes it much easier to replay or share the presentation without making it again each time.

Additionally, a new Captured by Me collection gathers photos you took with the Camera app, including shots captured on previous devices. The same criteria can also be used as a filter elsewhere in your library.

And photographers who want another way to organize their work, Photos adds one-to-five-star ratings. Ratings can then be used to filter the main library and collections. Just be sure to enable star ratings in Photos app settings as it’s off by default.

Faster uploads and better search

Lastly, two less visible changes could make Photos feel better in daily use.

macOS 27 lets you prioritize iCloud Photos syncing so new photos and videos begin uploading sooner.

This sounds especially useful when you’ve just imported a large batch and want it available on your other devices without waiting for lower-priority work.

Apple has also rebuilt the search foundation used by Spotlight, Photos, and Mail. Apple says the new system creates a more comprehensive index of your content and keeps it updated throughout the day, so that can only be positive.

macOS 27 Golden Gate improves how you share, organize, find, sync, present, and edit your photos. Together, these changes make for a more meaningful year for the app for regular Photos app users.

title: Out of Pocket: Detailing our everyday carry
snippet: I love building a “kit,” a “pack,” a bag with enough stuff in it to make sure I am ready for every eventuality. I’m not talking about a survival kit per se, just some things that mean I am basically ready for any modern situation. more…
fullText:
I love building a “kit,” a “pack,” a bag with enough stuff in it to make sure I am ready for every eventuality. I’m not talking about a survival kit per se, just some things that mean I am basically ready for any modern situation.

EDC or Every Day Carry is basically part of my personality at this stage. It started with smartphones, moved on to earbuds, and steadily, like many of you, I accrued an assortment of gadgets, products, and things I found myself dragging with me everywhere.

I am constantly on the lookout for the next thing to enhance my EDC. I’m not alone in this; Andrew is in the same boat. We’re product people first and foremost, but practicality has to be a component before it becomes a bigger part of daily lives.

We figured that we’d share some of that intimate knowledge, driven by building packs for trade shows, travel, and just, well, hanging around.

	

So, this is Out of Pocket, our new series diving into what makes our EDC tick. Expect more deep dives into the kinds of things that are adjacent to your smartphone, the things that you carry every day, or brand new products that might pique your interest. After all, we all have our own specific EDC essentials. Here are a few of ours to hopefully get your own creative juices flowing…

My current kit (Damien)

The Sidebag – TomToc T33 (3.5L)

My search for the perfect sidebag has been, I’ll be honest, arduous. Day-to-day, I’m not much of a backpack guy, so a sling or a sidebag is the perfect accessory for all the little things I feel like I need. I already own a Bellroy Venture Ready sling, and while it’s awesome. It is just a little bit too small for a real EDC kit.

TomToc’s T33 sidebag is exponentially better with more pockets, exceptional internal organization, and interior sections. You could fit a small-ish water bottle or drink in the middle section, but netted segments mean I can throw in paracetamol or lip balm for easy access. There’s enough room for a really small tablet or notebook and documents in the back portion.

There’s a key carabiner so I can throw in my house keys and keychain right at the front. It’s stretchy enough to open a door and have the key snap back into the front pocket.

One of my must-haves on a sling is a body-facing “secret” pocket. When I’m traveling, my passport goes here so it’s accessible, but also harder for someone to try and slip their hand in – not that this has been a problem.

One of the most important things for me is that it’s waterproof. While it’s hot right now in England, we’re due a downpour. I like that all my stuff inside is safe and dry. The zippers are smooth, with waterproof seams, and there are lots of carabiner anchor points too, so you can attach a hat or a water bottle. It hits all the right notes, and I’ve abused it thoroughly, and it just wipes clean.

It’s super cheap for what it offers at under $45. My only gripe is that the color options aren’t all that extensive, but you could level that criticism at basically any sidebag. This is one that won’t break the bank.

Get the TomToc T33 sling

The Juice  – Anker Nano 5,000mAh power pack

Power banks are just so ubiquitous now that you can basically boil it down to what you want or need. Because I use the Pixel 11 Pro, I always want a Magsafe-compatible power bank around to slap to the back of the phone.

I had been using the Genki Energy Pack for almost a year now, and there were a number of reasons for that. Firstly, it looks awesome with the black and orange color scheme. Secondly, it’s Qi2 certified, so it does all the necessary handshake stuff required to get faster and more efficient charging speeds.

However, it’s blocky and bulky, so I switched it out recently for something a little lighter. I’m rocking the Anker Nano power bank now because it isn’t as bulky and has enough juice to give me a full charge on basically any phone I’m carrying.

There’s a tiny strip of LEDs that shows remaining battery level; it’s Qi2 certified, but that is limited to 15W. I use the solitary USB-C charging port if I need 20W and above, but most of the time it’s absolutely fine when you’re out and about. For what it’s worth, I carry a super short USB-C cable that’s like 10cm for that specific reason too.

I do think it’s a little pricey, but you can get it in different colours and mine has taken a beating over the year or slightly longer I’ve been using it. It’s just something that can slip on to the back of your phone without being huge or messing around with cables – which is something I appreciate.

Get the Anker Nano power bank

On-the-go entertainment – Boox Go 6 e-reader

I reviewed the Boox Go 6 e-reader almost two years ago, and since then, it has become a staple in my EDC setup. It’s just so small and inconspicuous that it basically lives in my sidebag.

As an e-reader, it’s nothing special. I’d even say it’s a little underpowered for what it offers, but the size and shape are what keep me coming back basically every single day. I basically leave it running the Kindle app or download some epub files, and it handles those absolutely fine. It is technically an Android tablet, so you can share files using Quick Share. I find this is great if you find something you want to read because you can just fire things over without messing with cables. Heck, I have hundreds of EPUBs that just work now, which is lovely. Even PDFs work just fine.

It’s under 300g with a magnetic flip case attached, so it’s not heavy by any stretch of the imagination. I have my eye on a few of the even smaller Magsafe e-readers, but at 6-inches this is like a pamphlet or an especially large coupon. Perfect for reading novels, documents, or even a downloaded webpage – not that I would recommend that!

A newer version has just been released that enables note-taking and various other improvements. I’m hoping to test drive that soon, but I have genuinely loved the compact design of the Go 6 and think I’d struggle to go back to a full-sized Kindle for that reason alone. It has come down in price to around $160, which isn’t cheap, but still not bad if you want something super small. That said, something even smaller might be better for just throwing into an even smaller sling bag…

Get the Boox Go 6 e-reader

Always available audio – USB-C earbuds

I simply hate not having some earbuds with me when I’m out of the house. I simply must be distracted with podcasts, YouTube Music, or if I want to take a call, I cannot live without a pair in my bag.

I usually have about 20 pairs of Bluetooth earbuds lying around my desk, but when the battery dies, they’re useless. I was so annoyed at a pair of buds dying mid-flight while traveling last year that I bought a random pair of USB-C earbuds from an airport vending machine to keep the music flowing. I think they’re from Xiaomi as there’s a little “Mi” logo embossed on the inline remote. I only paid like $16, but Belkin makes a pair that are $15 and reputable enough that I might pick up a pair as a spare.

Honestly, they sound fine. The threshold is that a pair of earbuds just needs to sound better than traffic or that dull airplane drone. These earbuds live in my bag as a last resort audio option, heck, they’re great to just share with someone if they’ve forgotten their own earbuds. They take up basically negligible space, too. When I’m done with them, I quickly wipe them with an alcohol pad, and they’re sterilized. Trust me, it’s worth having at least one backup option because the one time you need them, it’s a lifesaver. If you lose them, it’s not a big deal. Win-win in my book.

Get some cheap USB-C earbuds

Retro on the go – Gamesir Pocket Taco controller

If I’m taking a backpack, I usually try to make room for my Steam Deck or Switch 2, but if I’m going out for a few hours, I’ll usually stick to something much smaller. I love Gamesir’s range of controllers, but the Pocket Taco is one that, as a millennial gamer and Gameboy obsessive, I’m sticking with for now.

It clips onto your phone – don’t worry, it has rubber pads to stop scratches – and gives you real buttons to play games in portrait orientation like Nintendo intended back in the late 1980s. It really does feel like a DMG Game Boy in the best ways. Thankfully, there are more buttons that you can map so that you can play other emulators, not just Gameboy.

If you’re not a gamer, mobile or otherwise, this might not be for you, and that’s absolutely fine. For nerds of a certain “vintage,” you’ll probably love this as much as I do.

Get the Pocket Taco game controller

The extras – ‘stuff’ and ‘things’

We’re all humans, so we can’t just have cables and batteries in our bags. I carry a few other key things that are useful. Most of these are just cheap things that I’ve found are worth having.

After a trip to a city with questionable-quality streetlights, I picked up a little keychain torch that just attaches to my keys. Olight makes a ton of EDC lighting products, but I love the iMini 2 at just $20 because it can just go on my keys with the carabiner clip.

I just charge it every couple of months using the integrated USB-A plug at the back, and it lasts a lotng time despite the fact that it’s absolutely tiny. Detach to power on, then it magnetically snaps back into place, and the light turns off. Super useful if you don’t want to drain your smartphone’s battery, and it’s bright enough to light a small room. Sometimes I just use it to fine stuff I’ve dropped down the side of my car seats.

Get the Olight iMini 2 keychain flashlight

I have spilled tea and coffee on my clothes so many times that I started carrying around a Tide stain pen a while back, and it has saved many a shirt. It’s not going to get out huge stains, but it’s still nice to stop something from ruining your outfit. They’re around $15 for a 5-pack. I can’t recommend them highly enough because they’ve stopped so many of my shirts and t-shirts from getting completely ruined over the past few years.

On a similar note, I try to carry a microfiber cleaning cloth, alcohol cleaning pads, and napkins or tissues. Throw in some hand gel, lotion, a little sunscreen, and I’m covered for basically any eventuality.

My current kit (Andrew)

The backpack – Peak Design Travel Backpack 20L

Whether I step outside with a sling or my backpack is entirely down to whether I decide to tote my laptop along. I use a MacBook Air 13-inch, which has the smallest footprint one can reasonably expect a bag to fit. But even so, there is a true limit to the number of slings that can carry a small laptop. So if that’s coming with me, I’m taking the Peak Design Travel Backpack 20L.

The 20L variant has easily become my favorite backpack to lug around if I’m going with a heavier loadout. It weighs very little, and it’s completely unassuming. If there needs to be more on my back, it can expand slightly beyond that small capacity. But otherwise, I’m able to carry my laptop and a few essentials without worry.

The main compartment is great for just throwing random items in. When I’m using this bag, stuff doesn’t need to be organized as it would in a dedicated camera bag. I’m generally going to bring my tech pouch along, too. But that’s almost overkill because the top pocket has all of the same inner pockets for those little things I want to tag along.

It has all of the little creature comforts you’d want. Magnetic strap keepers, a pass-through for luggage handles, and an internal water bottle holder, so a giant container of liquid isn’t sloshing around way off balance. Overall, it’s simple but incredibly effective at what it does.

Get the Peak Design Travel 20L

The sidebag – Bellroy Lite Sling Mini

As for the sling, my rule states that I’ll swap to this if my laptop isn’t coming along. The Sling Lite Mini has the feel of an outdoor bag without so much of the look, so it flies under the radar more than a technical pack might. The outer material is strong and lightweight, but it doesn’t repel liquid as well as I’d hope it would. The internal pocket structure is simple, but efficient. The main pocket is plenty large enough for random items, and it’s complemented by a zipper pocket for thinner items. One of the gussets that let it expand is lined with a pocket I use to slip my Nomad titanium pen and handy USB ChargeKey. On the other side, I clip my knife and flashlight.

The best part about it being geared towards outdoor use is that it’s expandable. The gusseted construction keeps it compact, no matter how much you stuff in it. So even if it’s full, the shoulder strap pulls it tight so the overall profile is kept slim.

It’s tough and just easy to grab and go. I love this bag.

Neither is traditionally “cheap,” and Damien offers a great alternative with his TomToc sidebag. But at $79 for the sling and double that for the Travel Backpack, it’s a “buy it for life” sort of purchase.

Get the Bellroy Sling Lite Mini

The power – Baseus Qi2 25W

I generally don’t have the fear of running out of power with whatever phone I’m using. I wouldn’t say I’m an ultra-power user, but there are times when I just start to run out of steam on my Galaxy Fold 8 Ultra or Pixel 11. You can carry a slim charging brick, which I do anyway, or you can take a magnetic power bank.

I always carry the Baseus 10,000mAh Qi2.2 25W power bank with me. Because the Pixel has magnets on the back without the help of a case, I can always slap it on. If needed, I can plug the bank into something else via USB-C. Speeds aren’t really an issue, either, because it runs at 25W – right where the Pixel 10 Pro XL is rated, even if it doesn’t always charge that fast.

Baseus has slightly thinner options, but I prefer the charging speed I get with the 25W model. It just works when I need it, and it’s really not all that heavy.

Get the Baseus Qi2 power bank

The catalyst – Statik MagStak Pro USB-C cable

It’s kind of big, and it’s kind of bulky, but if I’m bringing a bag, I have little reason not to throw this in. Statik’s MagStack cable is a 100W magnetic cable that essentially coils itself back up every single time. It solves the issue of cables that are all over the place and are resistant to any coercion to get them back into shape.

I’ve been using the MagStack cable for the better part of a year, and it just refuses to lose it’s uniform appeal. I bring it with me whenever I can because it’s just easy to pack away, given you have the pocket space. title: Apple Notes adds a power user feature in iOS 27 that’s rare in other apps
snippet: Apple Notes in iOS 27 adds a variety of new features, including one that power users are sure to appreciate: section links. more…
fullText:
Apple Notes in iOS 27 adds a variety of new features, including one that power users are sure to appreciate: section links.

Apple Notes lets you link to specific sections of your note in iOS 27

There’s no shortage of third-party notes apps on the App Store. You can find everything from barebones note-takers to powerhouse productivity suites.

Apple Notes has long excelled at offering a minimalist, user-friendly interface while also providing tools that power users love.

And in iOS 27, Notes has an exciting new addition in the latter category: section links.

Whenever you select some text inside a note in iOS 27 and open the edit menu, tapping ‘Add Link’ will reveal a new option: Link to Section.

Inside this menu, you’ll find a full list of all the headings and subheadings in your note. Tap one, and Notes will create a link to that specific section. You can choose to use the section title as the link’s text, or your own custom text.

Section links are great for navigating long notes, as they make it quick and easy to jump to a specific area.

With section links you can create a full-blown table of contents at the top of your note, or just use them sparingly for sections you revisit a lot.

Most iPhone owners probably won’t ever use the feature. But for power users who value more flexibility in their notes app, section links in Apple Notes are a welcome new addition.

title: The Quantified Scientist tests the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart rate sensor
snippet: In a new video, The Quantified Scientist’s Rob ter Horst compares the new Apple Watch Series 12’s heart rate sensor against a Polar H10 ECG chest strap. Here’s what he found. more…
fullText:
In a new video, The Quantified Scientist’s Rob ter Horst compares the new Apple Watch Series 12’s heart rate sensor against a Polar H10 ECG chest strap. Here’s what he found.

Revamped heart sensor delivers

For the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple completely revamped the device’s heart sensor, which now measures heart rate every five seconds even when the user isn’t active.

In our review of Apple Watch Series 12, which you can read here, we found that the added data can provide more detailed insights into how everyday activities and moments throughout the day affect heart rate, such as hauling groceries, doing yard work, drinking an afternoon cup of coffee, or dealing with a stressful moment at work.

That said, Rob ter Horst from The Quantified Scientist YouTube channel published an in-depth look (via MacMagazine) at the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart rate sensor during indoor cycling, running, and weightlifting, and compared its readings with those from a Polar H10 ECG chest strap.

All in all, the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart sensor performed very well, particularly during indoor cycling, where its readings were nearly identical to the Polar H10 data.

During a running session, the Series 12 also performed well, with a 0.98 correlation with the chest strap (versus a near-perfect correlation of 1.0 during indoor cycling), though ter Horst noted some minor deviations at higher heart rates.

During weightlifting, which ter Horst notes is traditionally one of the hardest activities for wrist-based heart rate sensors, the Series 12 posted the lowest correlation of the three exercises tested, at 0.97. Even so, ter Horst said the result was “quite good” compared with the competition, placing the Series 12 above 85% of devices he has tested for weightlifting.

Compared with his longer-term testing of the Apple Watch Series 11, ter Horst said the new Apple Watch Series 12 delivered broadly similar heart rate accuracy overall, with the older model actually performing slightly better during running in his tests. It could be the case, ter Horst notes, that Apple is still tweaking its algorithms for the new sensor.

Finally, ter Horst also tested the Apple Watch Series 12’s step counter. He manually counted roughly 5,000 steps and found the Series 12 was generally spot-on or only slightly overcounted.

title: Apple’s MLB Dodgers Live Broadcast Was Shot With iPhone 18 Pro Max
snippet: Around half of the cameras that shot the baseball game were new iPhone 18 Pro Max units, some of which sent footage over 5G.
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro Max units were spread strategically around the field of Dodger Stadium for the first Apple TV broadcast shot with iPhones that didn’t have sports lenses.

It was a beautiful night for a ballgame last Friday at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles — and some of the footage seen by viewers at home came right out of the phone in their pockets. 

That’s the iPhone 18 Pro Max in their pockets, if they happened to be one of the serious fans who bought one when it went on sale Friday. Apple’s latest iPhones have video upgrades with physical aperture blades and new modes, which fans watching the Dodgers take on the San Francisco Giants saw for themselves: Out of the 30 cameras shooting footage of the game, 14 were iPhone 18 Pro Max units. 

Several iPhone 18 Pro Max units were tucked into custom-made protective cushions to catch the game — and hopefully survive any unlucky foul balls rocketing their way.David Lumb/CNET

Ahead of the game, Apple brought members of the media, including me, to Dodger Stadium to see the setup, which would record footage for Apple TV Plus’s final broadcast of the Friday Night Baseball game. As soon as I stepped from the stands out onto the field, I found the first of these iPhones on a tripod just inside the dugout, pointed at the field. Considering the phone had only been released to the public that morning, it didn’t surprise me that the phone case for mounting it on the tripod read “iPhone 17 Pro Max.”

A total of three iPhone 18 Pro Max units were arranged behind the plate — two on either side slid into protective padding and one atop the pitch speedometer cameras.

Our tour continued behind the home plate, where iPhones were slotted into custom-made, heavy padding on the backstop and perched above the tower of pitch clock cameras. Others were placed in the visitors’ dugout, posted on the right-field foul pole and positioned toward the field from either team’s bullpens.

One perched on the wall above right-center field was on a gimbal, nicknamed “the robo” and manually controlled from the broadcast center, was positioned to capture outfielders rushing to the wall and reaching over to rob home runs. And one was carried out in the stands to get live fan reactions during the game.

The Ronin gimbal-mounted iPhone 18 Pro Max setup, seen in profile, perched just in front of right-center field, ready to catch game-making plays at the wall — and the crowd reaction behind it.David Lumb/CNET

Apple had its first live iPhone-shot broadcast of a Major League Soccer game back in May, but around half of the fifteen iPhone 17 Pro Max units were bolted onto large, professional-grade telephoto lenses. At Dodger stadium, all the iPhone 18 Pro Max units are shooting from their lenses alone. It’s a way to show off the differences in video capabilities on the premium phones, especially under the challenging conditions of night-time baseball games that start in daylight and end under stadium lights, explained Dylan Ashbrook, director of content and brand development for Apple Sports.

“The new 48MP Fusion Main camera gives us even more versatile video capabilities, and the variable aperture on the Main camera gives us another tool for managing exposure in-camera, giving us more control over the look of the game as conditions change,” Ashbrook said. 

Apple didn’t go into detail on the sixteen other cameras that shot the game, but presumably, they were conventional cameras with powerful telephoto lenses to capture plays up close. But the iPhones were chosen to capture angles that those hefty cameras couldn’t — because unlike them, nine of the iPhone 18 Pro Max units weren’t connected by cable wire to pipe in their live footage to the broadcast center. They sent it over wireless 5G — in the middle of the game.

An iPhone 18 Pro Max was positioned in visitor and home bullpens to capture close plays near the edge of the outfield.David Lumb/CNET

Live-streaming footage over 5G for a professional MLB broadcast

While five of the iPhones sent their footage through fiber cable to the broadcast center, nine sent theirs over a private 5G network, which T-Mobile set up ahead of the game. Apple tested the network and was confident there wouldn’t be any latency — in theory, it would be able to switch to any of the 14 iPhones around the stadium at any time. 

Not needing a bulky cable to send broadcast footage freed up Apple to place the iPhones in many more locations. That behind-the-plate setup only required Apple to get specially made backstop cushions (which met MLB safety standards) with small slots to slide an iPhone 18 Pro Max into, rather than arduously rebuilding the whole setup with wire connections. Not needing wires also enabled the free 360-degree movement of the gimbaled setup on the outfield wall.

It also means most of Apple’s setup for the game is intentionally temporary. When I asked the company’s representatives touring us around the field why they hadn’t put up an iPhone on the left-field foul pole, they noted that they could easily switch around the layout for the next game — including adding more gimbaled iPhones on the outfield wall, which they’re particularly excited about. 

The iPhone 18 Pro Max mounted above the speedometer — and cameras to capture spatial video.David Lumb/CNET

There’s one downside to the freedom of wireless iPhones: They won’t be plugged in to charge while they’re shooting video, which often drains the battery quickly. Since the iPhone 18 Pro Max units were shooting in 4K (which was later scaled down to 1080p in the broadcast center), and were streaming their footage to the broadcast center over 5G wireless, I was concerned about whether they’d last a whole game. While recent rule changes have shortened baseball games (last year’s average was around 2 hours and 40 minutes, according to MLB.com), that’s still a long stretch of continuous video.

Yet when I asked, Apple wasn’t worried. It was confident the iPhone 18 Pro Max units would last the whole game, no problem. (That’s also confidence that the phones wouldn’t overheat while recording video; temperatures topped out around 82 degrees F the day of the mid-September game). 

This iPhone 18 Pro Max unit is mounted inside the home team’s dugout, sitting alongside the World Series Champion players of the Dodgers.David Lumb/CNET

Apple’s likely right to feel secure that the iPhone 18 Pro Max wouldn’t run out of battery while shooting the games. The company never gives out exact capacities for the batteries on its iPhones, but has said that its latest and biggest phone should get last 30 hours on a full charge. In his review, CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland got about a day and a half of casual use before hitting 0% on the battery, and on a more intensive day of use, had 14% charge left just before midnight. 

I caught some of the game’s broadcast on Apple TV Plus, and while most of the broadcast stuck with the views that most viewers are familiar with (and were likely shot by conventional cameras) like looking over the pitcher’s shoulder toward the batter and bleacher-positioned zoom-ins on big plays, I did notice some iPhone footage snuck in there. 

Some of these were vantages at the field level of players and pitchers locked in to the game, but the biggest screentime came from the iPhone wandering around the stands getting the true fan experience. For viewers at home, this was definitely a new vantage from the seats they wished to be in, surrounded by jovial comrades adorned in Dodger blue.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile						
					

											

								

											David Lumb is a managing editor for the mobile team, covering mobile and gaming spaces. Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. As a true Californian, he lives for coffee, beaches and burritos.

title: AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27
snippet: AirPods just got a variety of new features in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3. Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
AirPods just got a variety of new features in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3. Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

GymKit can sync AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate data

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

Siri AI

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 will be Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

World Knowledge: “Ask about virtually any topic that’s on your mind, from important facts to recipes and restaurant recommendations. Siri AI can reference information online to give you detailed, up-to-date insights.”

Conversational: “Siri AI is your conversational AI assistant with entirely new capabilities…Ask open-ended questions, brainstorm ideas for work or creative projects on the go, and engage in natural, back-and-forth conversations.”

Personal Context: “Siri AI can find relevant answers to what you’re looking for just by asking. Search for a photo from years ago, easily locate an email buried in your inbox, or pull up a note you saved on your iPhone.”

Read more: AirPods keep getting better, and iOS 27’s biggest upgrade is Siri

Precision Finding via Apple Watch

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

title: GM just found the ‘sweet spot’ for supporting Android Auto & CarPlay [Gallery]
snippet: GM has been stubbornly standing by its decision to axe Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from many of its newer vehicles in recent years, despite loud and constant negative feedback from consumers. In its latest software update for two new trucks, GM has found the “sweet spot” for implementing Android Auto and CarPlay, but it’s unclear if that compromise will extend to other vehicles. more…
fullText:
GM has been stubbornly standing by its decision to axe Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from many of its newer vehicles in recent years, despite loud and constant negative feedback from consumers. In its latest software update for two new trucks, GM has found the “sweet spot” for implementing Android Auto and CarPlay, but it’s unclear if that compromise will extend to other vehicles. 

A new software experience – based on Android Automotive / Google built-in – debuting in the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado and 2027 GMC Sierra will see GM’s software not only get a nice new coat of paint, but also some welcome functionality. As detailed by CNBC, the update will “proactively surface relevant controls” such as call controls and even a garage door opener. Both vehicles have plenty of physical controls, too.

The biggest news here, though, is GM finding a new way to implement Android Auto and CarPlay integration.

GM announced in 2023 that it would remove phone projection systems from its vehicles while embracing Android Automotive and native functionality in its infotainment system, a decision that has not been positively embraced by customers. While GM has not backed down from this change on its electric vehicles, many of its vehicles still support both platforms. 

	

The change here is that the Silverado and Sierra will support Android Auto and CarPlay, but in a new windowed mode. The projection appears on a part of the display, with aspects of the native infotainment coming through around the sides so you can still easily control parts of the car that projection systems cannot without actually closing anything. 

Speaking to The Verge, GM group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles Colin McCormick explained that this is the “sweet spot.”

I think we’re landing in a spot where… we don’t have a customer that has to decide, “Oh, I’m going to use projection, or, oh, I want to use the native system…” That’s our sweet spot.

That said, there’s no word here on whether or not GM will actually bring Android Auto and CarPlay back to more of its vehicles. Gas-powered vehicles remain with support for phone projection, but that’s still missing in its EVs, including the latest Chevy Bolt that launched earlier this year.

title: This OMG Moment at the Doctor’s Made Me Take the Apple Watch Seriously
snippet: I was testing the Apple Watch’s ECG feature on video for CNET and as a healthy, active 30-year-old, the last thing I expected was to become part of the story.
fullText:
I haven’t always been a fan of the Apple Watch, thinking of it as an extraneous wearable novelty for years. That changed in 2018 when the Apple Watch Series 4 debuted with ECG. Looking at the watch’s tiny sensor, I didn’t believe that it could mimic the complex array of wires, stickers and monitors on hospital-grade electrocardiograms. So, I decided to put the Series 4’s ECG to the test alongside one at the hospital for a CNET story and video.  

As a healthy, active 30-year-old, the last thing I expected was to become part of the story.

An electrocardiogram measures your heart’s electrical signals, and it needs a complete electrical circuit. The Apple Watch closes that circuit with two electrodes: one on the back of the case, against your wrist, and one on the Digital Crown, against your finger. That’s one lead, compared to the 12 a hospital uses. Fewer leads, less detail, but still similar accuracy.

During the test, the Apple Watch showed the same pattern as the hospital ECG and flagged an irregular heartbeat. The cardiologist paused to review the results while I tried not to panic on camera.

The results from the Apple Watch ECG showed the same irregular beat as the doctor’s ECG and caused this “OMG” moment when my health became a part of the story.James Martin/CNET

After further testing, that early beat turned out to be benign, likely the result of stress and sleep deprivation from juggling a new baby and a full-time job. But in that “OMG” moment, I stopped seeing the Apple Watch as a vanity-metric machine and started seeing it as a tool to catch something happening in my heart before I could even feel it.

Years later, I gave my parents Apple Watches as a sort of insurance policy for fall detection and heart-health alerts. Last year, my dad’s watch flagged something that ultimately led to his diagnosis and treatment for a potentially life-threatening heart condition.

There are plenty of Apple Watch health stories like ours now, and I’m sure there will be more. But looking back, my original article and video feel like a snapshot of the exact moment my relationship with the Apple Watch changed.

And yes, the “does this mean I’m going to die?” moment in the video below was genuine.

title: Here’s what’s really going on with GM’s CarPlay strategy (or lack thereof)
snippet: Despite headlines to the contrary, GM isn’t changing its position on CarPlay and Android Auto support. The automaker is not bringing phone projection support back to any cars from which it has already been removed. Here’s what’s really happening. more…
fullText:
Despite headlines to the contrary, GM isn’t changing its position on CarPlay and Android Auto support. The automaker is not bringing phone projection support back to any cars from which it has already been removed. Here’s what’s really happening. 

No, GM isn’t walking back its decision to ditch CarPlay

The confusion started when GM announced a new software experience for its Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks last week. The company touted a new picture-in-picture phone mirroring system in which CarPlay and Android Auto would coexist alongside GM’s native infotainment system.

Some sources interpreted this news as GM backtracking on its plan to ditch CarPlay, which it first announced in 2023. Unfortunately, that is not the case. GM’s original announcement was about dropping CarPlay support from its future EVs. It has followed through on that plan, except for the Cadillac Lyriq EV.

GM has not removed CarPlay or Android Auto from any of its gas-powered cars. Therefore, the new phone projection system in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks is not the automaker caving to the pressure and bringing CarPlay support back to its EVs.

A GM spokesperson confirmed this to Joanna Stern, who posted the following on X today:

Correction: GM has confirmed it is NOT rolling phone projection to GM EVs. Instead this announcement is specific to JUST their new gas powered light-duty pickups, which have always supported Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The confusion is reasonable. GM CEO Mary Barra said in an interview that the automaker would remove CarPlay and Android Auto from gas cars at some point. The company quickly clarified, however, that gas cars would continue to offer phone projection “for the foreseeable future.”

All that’s to say, nothing has changed. GM isn’t bringing CarPlay back to its EVs. The company’s strategy has not changed. Perhaps we can interpret GM’s picture-in-picture solution for select gas cars as a sign that it’s aware the decision to ditch CarPlay is unpopular. I think that’s too favorable an interpretation, though.

title: WhatsApp starts rolling out new in-chat search button on iOS
snippet: Following a few weeks of beta testing, WhatsApp is now rolling out its new in-chat search button to iPhone users. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following a few weeks of beta testing, WhatsApp is now rolling out its new in-chat search button to iPhone users. Here are the details.

Early last month, WhatsApp started testing a new search button in the bottom-right corner of the in-chat interface, making it easier to start a search.

Up until now, in-chat search required users to tap on the contact or group name at the top of the conversation, select the search option from the chat info screen, and then enter their query after being taken back to the main chat.

An in-chat search button, by contrast, streamlines the process by letting users start searching without leaving the conversation.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is officially rolling out the in-chat search button, though it appears in a different location than it did during beta testing.

Inage: WABetaInfo

Here’s WABetaInfo:

The new search button appears at the top of the screen when users scroll up through the conversation. When users return to the bottom of the chat, the button disappears again. It shows up contextually, only when it is useful. Users who see the button can tap it to activate search mode directly within the conversation. As soon as users enable search mode, they can type a keyword and find matching messages without leaving the chat. The search mode works just like the existing one, so users who are already familiar with it will not have to learn anything new.

WABetaInfo notes that the new shortcut is available across individual chats, group chats, and channels. In all three cases, the button appears near the top of the screen when users scroll up through the conversation or channel, and disappears again when they return to the bottom.

As with most WhatsApp feature rollouts, the new search button may take some time to reach everyone.

title: Apple didn’t give up on stylus support for iPhone Duo; Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold should take notes
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo may not have reinvented the Android foldable, but it certainly did put a polish on a number of things. Inlcuded in that list is stylus support on the iPhone Duo, something that was more complicated behind-the-scenes than it initially sounded like, and an effort that Samsung should probably take note of. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo may not have reinvented the Android foldable, but it certainly did put a polish on a number of things. Inlcuded in that list is stylus support on the iPhone Duo, something that was more complicated behind-the-scenes than it initially sounded like, and an effort that Samsung should probably take note of.

Rewinding, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold series first added stylus support back in 2022 on the Galaxy Z Fold 3. Samsung made a special version of the S Pen stylus for foldables that didn’t require a battery, but also didn’t stow away inside of the foldable. Still, it was fully supported and a welcome tool, especially as the Galaxy Note series was dying off. But with last year’s Galaxy Z Fold 7, Samsung ditched support for the S Pen in order to make the foldable much thinner.

S Pen support on Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Fold 5

But, of course, Samsung is likely rethinking that decision now that Apple has introduced the iPhone Duo with stylus support.

Apple touts that the iPhone Duo will support the USB-C version of the Apple Pencil that’s otherwise made for iPads. It sounds simple enough, but there’s more to the story. Bloomberg reports that Apple originally wanted to make a dedicated version of Apple Pencil for the iPhone Duo, a version that would have been shorter and able to magnetically hold itself on the Duo’s hinge. 

	

That stylus wasn’t announced as, apparently, Apple ran into “technical problems ahead of mass production” a few months before the Duo was announced, leading to the pivot over to iPad versions of the stylus. The report further notes that Apple’s software update to enable this isn’t “as simple as hitting a button” and that it won’t arrive until “fairly late in 2026.” 

Still, that’s more than Samsung is bringing to the table at this point. Both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra lack any support for a stylus, despite rumors of Samsung exploring other ways of offering a stylus on its foldables. The reason the traditional S Pen doesn’t work in these thin form factors is that it requires a physical layer in the display assembly and, as such, adds to the thickness and weight – two pillars that Samsung is hyper-focused on improving with each generation. 

Samsung’s Android competition has embraced stylus support, so between that and Apple’s adoption (mostly the latter, obviously), it’s all the more likely Galaxy Z Fold 9 will bring stylus support page in one form or another. Samsung has left the door open, too.

fullText:
If you’re anything like me, you’ve been all-in on smart lights for years. I almost never use light switches anymore and the luxury I’ve grown used to is immediately made apparent when I spend a night away from home. That said, smart lighting has continued to evolve far beyond the basic bulbs I’ve grown used to, and this was plain as day when I got my hands on the new Linkind Smart Light Stick.

First and foremost, these bulbs pack Matter compatibility for simple controls, but the perks really come to life when you tap into the AiDot app. This is where you can take advantage of addressable zones within the bulb, which sort of blew my mind. I also love the clean cylindrical look of these bulbs, which I will showcase down below.

The first thing that stood out to me when unboxing it was the hardware design. Rather than sticking to the familiar pear shape of standard household bulbs, Linkind opted for a clean, frosted cylinder. For this reason, I really think it will look great in frosted and transparent fixtures alike.

Matter-compatible bulbs with rich app customization

The setup process was refreshingly straightforward. As shown in the screenshots, grabbing the AiDot app and running through the pairing sequence took about a minute or so, and I was relieved straight away when I saw that the app actually had solid ratings. While Matter certification allows users to skip third-party apps entirely, skipping AiDot would cause you to miss out on a lot of the features that an app like AiDot can offer.

	

As you can see below, the number of available scenes is sort of obscene. It was a little overwhelming to see the number of options, but it’s easy to create favorites, which I’ll certainly be doing so it is easy to switch for whatever holiday season we are in the middle of.

To put these bulbs through their paces, I installed them across three different fixtures. First up was the pergola and hot tub area. Transparent wall mounted lanterns along the white lattice frame gave the Light Sticks plenty of room to show off. I then added them to one of the lamp posts in my yard, followed by the lamp that resides in my home office.

Hero feature is the customizable flame effect

Easily the coolest trick up the Light Stick’s sleeve is its built-in flame simulation. Rather than settling for a basic pixelated flicker, the frosted cylindrical design diffuses light to deliver a much more authentic look than I tend to see with other bulbs, especially when dropped into an open fixture like my office lamp or outdoor lanterns.

Setup is straight forward, allowing me to quickly customize the look I was after. I did my best to capture it in action in the video below. In my opinion, the video doesn’t quite do it justice, as I think it looks much better in person.

Seasonal curb appeal with festive scenes

Until now, I’ve been going with warm white lighting 100% of the time. With Linkind Smart Light Stick Pro, I don’t have a reason to forego shaking up the look of my space when the seasons change or a holiday arrives.

While there are plenty of pre-made dynamic scenes to pick from, the DIY tab in the AiDot app is where the hardware really shines. As mentioned earlier, there are individually addressable zones, offering up 50 individual areas you can customize. I was able to use the app to create a neat color effect in under a minute, and you can see the UI below.

The settings above lead to another neat animation that I tried to capture on video. Like before, while it looks great on video, it’s even better in person. I took the lamp shade off and you can see that the bulb looks great even when fully on display, which is something I cannot say for a lot of the other smart bulbs out there.

And if you want clearer examples of what the bulbs actually look like in person, check out the official footage in the video below. It highlights a wider variety of dynamic presets, from festive holiday scenes to subtle ambient glows. It really drives home just how versatile these are compared to standard, single-color smart bulbs.

Pricing and availability

If you want to step up your outdoor or indoor lighting like I have, head over to Linkind’s website to find these bulbs (and all of the others they sell). You can pick up the bulbs directly on Amazon, where they are currently selling for $39.99.

title: John Ternus just gave the best defense yet for Vision Pro
snippet: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus recently sat down for a lengthy, in-depth interview with French outlet Clique TV, and in it he gave the best defense yet for Apple Vision Pro. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new CEO John Ternus recently sat down for a lengthy, in-depth interview with French outlet Clique TV, and in it he gave the best defense yet for Apple Vision Pro.

John Ternus compares Vision Pro to the earliest days of personal computers

Apple Vision Pro is an oddity in Apple’s hardware lineup. It isn’t commercially successful the way the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and AirPods are. But the device is a technological marvel, and has garnered a small base of loyal fans who love it.

In the past, Tim Cook defended Vision Pro’s underwhelming sales by saying it’s an “early adopter product.”

Now John Ternus has weighed in, and I found his answer a more satisfying reason for Vision Pro to exist.

In a new interview, Clique TV’s Mouloud Achour asked Ternus: “The Vision Pro: for you is it a test, a flop, or the first step to the future of what’s going to be…a computer?”

Here’s what Ternus said:

Vision Pro to me is an amazing device. It’s an absolutely amazing device. But I think of it as like the early days of computers. It is the early days of a long journey. That’s how I feel about Vision Pro. What you see, if you think about the early days, people found different reasons where the computer allowed them, the Mac allowed them to do something never before possible. Like desktop publishing, and it became a big thing in that industry. 

What you’re seeing with Vision Pro now is, certainly there’s early adopters who love it and they’re using it and they’re enjoying it, but you also—surgeons are starting to use it in surgery because it’s just a fundamentally better tool for them than a monitor that’s kind of sitting over here. And so it’s growing in that area. In film production people are using it for set development and things like that. So we’re going to continue to grow and find more and more compelling use cases. And I think there’s a very bright future.

Ternus invokes Cook’s language of citing early adopters, but his comparison to the early days of computing is also helpful.

	

When personal computers first came on the scene, they were very expensive and had extremely limited use cases. But over time that changed, eventually unlocking possibilities that could scarcely have been imagined in the early days.

The dream of lightweight glasses offering full-fledged “spatial computing” features may be several years away. But it’s easy to see that future coming true, and the Vision Pro being a key part of that.

title: Pixel VIPs 2.0 redesign starts rolling out with fullscreen look
snippet: Following last week’s Feature Drop, Pixel VIPs 2.0 is beginning to roll out, and it brings more changes than just the widget redesign. more…
fullText:
Following last week’s Feature Drop, Pixel VIPs 2.0 is beginning to roll out, and it brings more changes than just the widget redesign.

With version 2.0, tapping on a contact in the widget no longer slides up a bottom sheet over your homescreen. Instead, it now opens a fullscreen layout, which was previously accessible by swiping up. The previous design was better for one-handed use as the call and message shortcuts were closer to the bottom of the screen.

Other changes to this page include a pencil icon in the top-right corner that lets you quickly edit in Google Contacts, while the call, message, video, and contact buttons now use outline-style icons.

Old vs. new

	

Google has moved the “Local updates” card to the top spot over “Last connection,” while “Notes” is now the last section as Pixel VIPs has removed the media and place recommendations.

Meanwhile, the big update today is a new pill-shaped switcher that shows all your VIPs. This allows for quick switching without having to go back to the homescreen.

The actual widget redesign is not yet live after updating to Pixel VIPs 2.0. However, there is a preview of the new layout with “space for quick actions” that lets you call and message directly from the widget.

Pixel VIPs 2.0 is widely rolled out via the Play Store.

title: New Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 fitness feature is surprisingly motivating
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new fitness-tracking feature: live step tracking on the watch face. Alongside live heart rate data, it’s a surprisingly welcome and motivating change to the new hardware that I’m loving so far. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new fitness-tracking feature: live step tracking on the watch face. Alongside live heart rate data, it’s a surprisingly welcome and motivating change to the new hardware that I’m loving so far.

Conceptually, step tracking data on the watch face is a rather unremarkable feature. Third-party apps like Pedometer++ have long been able to display your step count on your watch face. But Apple has waited until Series 12 and Ultra 4 to build in support for the Apple Watch.

Step tracking data has always been collected by Apple Watch. Even your iPhone can measure step tracking throughout the day, dating back to the iPhone 5s (before the Apple Watch existed). 

Before Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, however, Apple tucked step tracking data away inside apps like Fitness and Health. Now, it’s a built-in complication option from the Fitness app, just like activity rings. 

My guess is that Apple didn’t surface this data before for a two reasons. First, Apple’s new hardware is more capable and more efficient. That must be the reason why live step data is hardware-specific.

Second, I think Apple has liked the idea of presenting the Apple Watch as more comprehensive than just step tracking. The heart rate monitor and other sensors tell a much more complete story than just steps walked per day.

Whatever the thinking may have been before, we now have built-in live step tracking on the Apple Watch face. And the result? For me at least, it’s a surprisingly motivating number to view so far.

While I most appreciate live heart rate data for real-time insight, I’m finding that little step tracking number to be most beneficial when I start my day. It’s basically a race to get out of the hundreds and into the thousands. Otherwise that triple-digit number is just staring me down all day. 

My current strategy is to knock out a 16-minute rolling hills workout on my GymKit-equipped BowFlex T6 treadmill early in the day. This adjusts incline up and down, allowing me to focus on speed and a fixed session time. The sooner I knock out the mile run, the more time for a cooldown walk afterwards.

It’s also just really satisfying to watch the number increase as you walk, even if you’re not logging a workout. It’s a small thing, but it’s a welcome new way to gamify increasing your activity, especially if you’re anchored to a desk for much of the day.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are both available now. You can read the 9to5Mac review here.

title: Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid
snippet: An overwhelming sense of familiarity struck me the first time I used a Googlebook. That was immediately followed by a realization that this is just Android, and I think that feeling of similarity will go a long way in justifying and ultimately selling Googlebooks. more…
fullText:
An overwhelming sense of familiarity struck me the first time I used a Googlebook. That was immediately followed by a realization that this is just Android, and I think that feeling of similarity will go a long way in justifying and ultimately selling Googlebooks.

Going into this event, I was not particularly asking for a desktop operating system that felt like my Pixel phone. In fact, having used Chromebooks for many years (my first unit was the 2013 Acer C720), I thought Googlebook OS would not feel too different from ChromeOS. The desktop and app dock look the same, but the changes made by building on top of Android make all the difference.

That shared design and user experience allowed me to immediately start using Googlebook OS like a near-expert. Quick Settings and Notifications were obviously in the top-right corner, matching Android’s conventions. It’s a small change compared to ChromeOS, but it felt natural the first time I used it. I knew immediately to move the cursor to that top corner instead of the usual bottom corner on Chromebooks.

I also knew I could add and edit widgets, a long-requested feature ChromeOS lacks, by long-pressing on the desktop, while seeing the same ones from my phone homescreen evoked an almost nostalgia-like feeling.

	

The Settings app is identical to that on Pixel phones, while I was very happy to find Pixel Weather (and its widgets) along with the excellent Recorder pre-installed. Meanwhile, the app drawer is basically the Pixel Launcher. Compared to ChromeOS, you can put apps, widgets, and files/folders on the desktop for an infinite boost to productivity.

The best of the web 

Given how much Googlebook OS felt like using my Pixel phone, it was surprising to see that launching Gmail and Google Calendar opened the web versions rather than the Android apps. Talking with Google, I later learned that these were Trusted Web Activities (TWAs) instead of PWAs. Distributed from the Play Store, their main advantage is how this web wrapper-esque format allows for homescreen widgets.  

Zooming out, what shocked me was how much Googlebook OS leverages web apps, a move that strongly affirms the ChromeOS lineage. Going in, I assumed there would be a resurgence in desktop-class Android apps. 

However, I am told this was an intentional choice. Google’s viewpoint is ultimately to let app developers decide what the best strategy is for their application, and I think that’s fair. Google offered me the example of how it approached the Gmail and Workspace teams about whether they wanted to offer Googlebook adopters the web version or the Android app. They chose the former and ideally did not want to offer the Android app as an available Play Store download.

However, I do think this is partially a missed opportunity. Giving third-party developers a choice does reduce the barrier to entry for a new OS, but I strongly think Google internally should have enforced a strict first-party mandate to create desktop-class applications. 

Meanwhile, as I complained about in my Pixel Tablet review three years ago, it’s unbelievable that Google Messages is still using the same web-based version rather than anything more native. 

The Chrome browser on Googlebooks feels great and offers a full-featured experience from extensions to the new vertical tab list.

For all Android, always

That said, other experiences are clearly Android-powered. This includes the Google app and Gemini. When you invoke the Magic Pointer overlay, prompt responses appear in the Android Gemini app.

More broadly, Google sees this Android-based OS as an opportunity to leverage the existing Gemini and AI work done for phones as a starting point for the desktop. This is compared to having to rebuild everything from scratch for ChromeOS.

The on-device AI model is Gemini Nano, and that’s used to power AI descriptions of your screenshots that unlock search, as well as Magic Pointer, Rambler, and Create My Widget via a hybrid intelligence architecture.

I have to use the much-derided Magic Pointer a bit more to determine whether it’s some groundbreaking UX paradigm, but I do credit it for being very easy to enable. You will not forget that this feature exists on Googlebooks, and I think that could be valuable.

Rambler is the other major Gemini Intelligence feature, and you launch it from a Quick Insert key that’s in place of Caps Lock. Pressing the new Quick Insert key launches a rather convenient floating window that provides quick access to emoji, recent screenshots, and the Gboard clipboard, with Rambler in the bottom-right corner. This is a rather smart carryover from ChromeOS, now accessible with a single key press rather than a three-key combo.

Create My Widget is the other major tentpole. This is the introduction of generative UI to Android, and I think the ramifications for the future are tremendous. Right now, you get to make widgets that pull from live data sources, like Search. Googlebooks will definitely have to guide people on how to use this capability, but I think this could be a powerful selling point.

Google is adopting the successful Android OEM model for Googlebooks. However, they’ve fortunately drawn a line on how updates will work. Google is responsible for rolling out Googlebook OS updates, not OEMs, carrying over one of the strongest elements of ChromeOS. Partners will be able to specify preloaded apps, but they can’t do any heavy customization like altering what the status bar icons look like. The experience of using a Googlebook will be universal across partners. 

	

Google will be releasing major Googlebook OS updates on a quarterly basis to match the Android Quarterly Platform Release (QPR) model, but security updates can come at any time in between. 

Closing

Google spent a long time developing Googlebooks, and it shows. The specific example that really surprised me is that Google built an Antigravity app with native UI for Android. Going in, I thought they would just offer the Linux version, but this Antigravity for Android is distributed via the Play Store and interacts with the Linux terminal environment on Googlebook OS.

Frankly, Google fumbled its initial unveiling of Googlebooks in May. It was officially intended only as a preview, but the decision to highlight only a handful of features, including Magic Pointer, ended up being a great disservice. Googlebook OS is so much more than that, and the company should have led with the Android nature right off the bat.

Again, we actually have to see if it works in our daily workflows, but my initial impression is that Android gives Googlebooks a very solid foundation.

title: Apple is taking a little bit of a gamble with iPhone Duo software: Will it pay off?
snippet: With the new iPhone Duo, Apple is taking a little bit of a software gamble. All apps, in order to take advantage of the larger inner display of iPhone Duo, will need to be recompiled for iOS 27.0 at a minimum. To use the Duo’s unique new tab bar and other UI components, you’ll need iOS 27.1. Of course, this means a lot of developers will have to rebuild to support the Duo. On the flip side, it also means Apple is taking a risk of many apps on iPhone Duo being stuck in black bars. more…
fullText:
With the new iPhone Duo, Apple is taking a little bit of a software gamble. All apps, in order to take advantage of the larger inner display of iPhone Duo, will need to be recompiled for iOS 27.0 at a minimum. To use the Duo’s unique new tab bar and other UI components, you’ll need iOS 27.1.

Of course, this means a lot of developers will have to rebuild to support the Duo. On the flip side, it also means Apple is taking a risk of many apps on iPhone Duo being stuck in black bars.

One obvious solution would’ve been for Apple to allow iPad binaries that support resizing to run on iPhone Duo. The compromise here is that it’d likely feel a little more janky. Many developers would also likely take longer to support the iPhone Duo interface elements if they had a compatibility layer.

I get why Apple didn’t do that, because the interface they designed for iPhone Duo is genuinely intuitive, and it makes it feel like a lot of care went into the product. If Apple supported resizable iPad apps, it’d feel a lot more like any other Android foldable.

That said, you have to wonder how long some developers will take to at least compile for iOS 27. Compiling for iOS 27 doesn’t just mean you have to support the Duo, but it also means you’ll no longer have the compatibility option to opt-out of supporting Liquid Glass. For developers who haven’t prepared, the latter likely means many will drag their feet on iPhone Duo updates.

Seeing as you can split screen apps on the Duo, apps not fully expanding on the inside display might not be the biggest deal. That is, if Apple supports split screen with non-native apps.

However, for mobile gaming, a use case I’m sure will be very popular on the inside screen on the iPhone Duo, not having a proper full screen experience would be a major deterrent for many users.

I do hope Apple’s efforts to encourage developers to support the Duo’s interface work out, though I do genuinely worry. Obviously, we’ll see how things pan out with enough time.

Worst case scenario, Apple could simply add an iPad app compatibility mode to iPhone Duo in iOS 28, as a means of improving the experience for users while also getting all of the initial wave of support.

I am genuinely excited for iPhone Duo, though Apple’s gamble on getting third party developers to support Liquid Glass and the Duo at the same time might cause a rough experience for the first few months.

title: Here’s why Apple scrapped its shorter Apple Pencil designed for iPhone Duo: report
snippet: Leading into the iPhone Duo launch, we heard from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman that Apple was considering a new Apple Pencil for iPhone Duo, though it was unlikely that the company would go forward with it. Of course, the iPhone Duo keynote came, and Apple did announce support for the USB-C Apple Pencil. Here’s how that happened. more…
fullText:
Leading into the iPhone Duo launch, we heard from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman that Apple was considering a new Apple Pencil for iPhone Duo, though it was unlikely that the company would go forward with it. Of course, the iPhone Duo keynote came, and Apple did announce support for the USB-C Apple Pencil. Here’s how that happened.

Apple Pencil support was reportedly always on the roadmap for iPhone Duo, and the company had designed the product to be compatible. That said, the company had initially planned to build a new Apple Pencil for the Duo. It would’ve been smaller and attached to the hinge side of the iPhone Duo.

According to Bloomberg, that pencil ran into “technical problems” prior to mass production, so the company scrapped it and went with the traditional USB-C Apple Pencil.

After the keynote, you might’ve noticed on Apple’s website that Apple Pencil support won’t be available on iPhone Duo at launch. That delay is a result of the fact that the product wasn’t initially designed with the USB-C Apple Pencil in mind, and Apple still needs to test it thoroughly:

But getting the iPad Pencils to work on the iPhone Duo isn’t as simple as hitting a button to enable support. Apple has to roll out new software to make them compatible and run loads of internal tests. That process is now underway within Apple, with the company — as it said during the Duo unveiling — believing that support will be ready by the end of the year. I would take that literally: It will be fairly late in 2026.

It’s not quite clear if the technical problems with the new Apple Pencil design are with the Apple Pencil, or if it’s with the iPhone Duo being able to magnetically charge it. If it’s the former, it’s certainly possible that Apple will still debut the accessory at a later date.

title: Former Apple retail chief’s new ‘Shop Different’ book now available
snippet: Ron Johnson, Apple’s former senior vice president of retail operations, is out with a new book today called ‘Shop Different: How Retail Revealed Apple’s Genius.’ In the book, Johnson tells the story of working alongside Steve Jobs to craft Apple’s retail strategy. more…
fullText:
Ron Johnson, Apple’s former senior vice president of retail operations, is out with a new book today called ‘Shop Different: How Retail Revealed Apple’s Genius.’

In the book, Johnson tells the story of working alongside Steve Jobs to craft Apple’s retail strategy.

‘Shop Different,’ written with Zander Nethercutt, isn’t a “traditional business book,” but rather an “insider account of one of the most important retail successes of our time.”

Here’s the description:

When Steve Jobs hired Ron Johnson to create the Apple Store in 2000, con­ventional wisdom said that the inter­net would put stores out of business. By the time he left Apple in 2011, Johnson and his team had created the most respected and profitable retail stores in the world. And even then, skeptics were still predicting the death of physical retail.

In Shop Different, Johnson reveals how it happened: how he earned Jobs’s trust, how they developed a vision for a store that would win not by selling but by serving, and how he convinced Jobs that the store’s service philosophy should be rooted in some­thing as intangible as love. Johnson then gives readers a new look at Apple’s ascent to the most valuable company in the world; offers an inspiring vision for a future in which retailers win on connection, service, and experience; and shares an honest look at what leads to success—and what can follow.

Johnson joined 9to5Mac’s Overtime podcast last week to discuss ‘Shop Different’ and the origins of the Apple Store. Jeff and Fernando did an excellent job interviewing Johnson, and you can watch it on YouTube, or listen via Apple Podcasts and other platforms.

‘Shop Different: How Retail Revealed Apple’s Genius’ can be ordered on Amazon today. You can also order it and support local bookstores via Bookshop.org. My copy arrives today and I’m looking forward to diving in.
