title: Space Is More Crowded Than Ever. How Much More Can It Take?
snippet: From portable radars in shipping containers to orbital cameras, I asked scientists how the space-junk tracking industry plans to avoid catastrophic crashes.
fullText:
Key takeaways 

Orbital congestion: Nearly 17,000 active satellites raise serious concerns about potential orbital collisions and Kessler syndrome.

Tracking technology: Ground-based portable radars and in-orbit cameras monitor space debris, though tracking objects under 10 centimeters remains difficult.

Communication barriers: The main obstacle to space safety is the lack of open data sharing among competing entities and adversarial nations.

Walking inside LeoLabs’ new space radar nestled in the Maui hills felt like entering a computer. Wires dangled overhead, servers whined, and the temperature climbed in the metal box as the air conditioning leaked out when we entered. 

“You don’t want to be in there when the whole thing’s running,” said Matthew Adelman, LeoLabs’ senior manager of radar systems. “Not just for the safety, but also for the noise.”

Called Scout-S, this radar designed to track space objects is the size of a 20-foot shipping container and can be transported anywhere in the world. You can hook it up to an electrical grid and fiber internet, but its real calling card is portability. You could drop the Scout-S off-grid and have it running in a couple of hours. All you need is a generator and a Starlink dish to feed the radar’s data back to a computer.

I couldn’t help but appreciate the irony at the mention of the Starlink dish: The satellite internet service revolutionized the space industry, but it also jump-started a race to space that created the need for transportable radars like the Scout-S. 

The Soviet Union launched the world’s first satellite in 1957; it would take another 53 years for the population to pass 1,000. When Starlink launched its first satellite in 2019, there were still only around 2,000 orbiting Earth. Today, we’re at 16,810, and nearly 2 out of every 3 belong to Starlink. 

Each one of them is zooming above us at 17,000 mph. A collision between two of them could range from extremely troubling to catastrophic. Worst-case scenario, satellites colliding with each other or a piece of space debris could set off a feedback loop known as Kessler syndrome, in which one collision creates thousands of new pieces of debris that cause yet more collisions. It could ultimately make low Earth orbit, or LEO, the sweet spot where Starlink beams down fast, low-latency internet from 342 miles over our heads, so filled with space junk that it’s no longer usable. 

“We worry a lot about it because we have seen that in the last few years, the number of spacecraft has increased exponentially, and we are not stopping it,” said Lorenzo Olivieri, a professor at the University of Padova. I spoke with him this week at the Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference, where he was presenting a paper on space debris populations from break-up events.

“The worrisome idea of the Kessler syndrome could be a real close future,” Olivieri said. 

Exactly how worried you should be about a Kessler syndrome-like scenario depends on who you ask. When I polled scientists at AMOS, their answers ran the gamut. Some said it’s only a matter of time if we stay on our current trajectory, while others waved it off as the domain of science fiction. (See the 2013 movie Gravity for a particularly vivid dramatization.)

But you don’t have to be a Kessler syndrome pessimist to take crowded orbits seriously. Whether you’re a satellite operator looking to avoid collisions or the US military deploying space weapons, everyone at AMOS wants to know what’s going on in the skies. The industry, referred to as space situational awareness, is estimated to reach $1.9 billion this year. 

Aside from dodging millions of pieces of satellite-killing debris, operators also have to communicate with each other about where and when they’ll be moving. It’s an enormous challenge: How do you get adversarial nations and competing companies to agree on appropriate behavior in space? 

“Driving on the highway would be terrifying if everyone had their eyes closed,” Gabriel Swiney, the director of policy at the US Department of Commerce’s Office of Space Commerce, told me. “The problem is communication and knowledge.”

The issues circulating the AMOS conference were as terrifying as space lasers and as mundane as standardizing space data for easier sharing. 

I was almost ready to write off these topics as niche industry concerns when I pulled my phone out to get directions back to my hotel. A GPS satellite zooming 12,550 miles over my head instantly showed me where I was and needed to go. 

Traffic cameras for the skies

One engineer at AMOS described space awareness to me as having three stages: collection, processing and analysis. Many of the companies hawking their wares at the conference dabbled in multiple phases, but for the most part, they specialized in one of these buckets.

LeoLabs’ Scout-S radar is designed to be transported and setup within hours anywhere in the world. Allyza Umali/CNET

LeoLabs, the company that developed the transportable Scout-S radar, is primarily in the collection business. It has a dozen radar sites around the world, some of which can detect debris as small as 10 centimeters – a dangerous blind spot for most trackers.

“Think about the busy part of Seattle,” says Darren McKnight, senior technical fellow at LeoLabs. “If you have two traffic cameras, you don’t really know what route to take. You want traffic cameras at all the major intersections.”

It’s not always tiny pieces of debris — sometimes companies are even trying to find their own satellites up there. SpaceX, the company that operates Starlink, landed its reusable Falcon 9 rocket for the first time in 2015, kicking off a wave of “rideshare” launches. 

Some of these had as many as 140 payloads, making it a challenge for satellite operators to even determine which ones were theirs. 

“Once the first rideshare launch became a thing, that just exploded the number of things in orbit pretty quickly,” said Belinda Marchand, chief scientist at Slingshot Aerospace. “It was no longer just one launch vehicle and one object. It was one launch vehicle and a hundred.”

LeoLabs’ traffic cameras are all based on the ground, but other companies use cameras in orbit to give them a more detailed account of what’s happening in space.

“We use cameras that are in space to take pictures of other satellites in space,” said Hilary Cohen, director of operations at HEO USA. “There are trackers that track the dots and you know exactly where those satellites are. But this lets us go a layer deeper.”

This photo from an HEO space camera shows a solar panel in an abnormal configuration.HEO USA

Google Maps for satellites

But even if companies and countries do a good job of gathering information about their orbital goods, sharing it with other operators is an entirely different challenge. The key piece of information that everyone needs is called “ephemeris,” which lists the position and velocity of an object in orbit.

“Ephemeris basically is like my Google Maps,” McKnight said. “You’re sending it to everybody on the road with you and saying, ‘Here’s where I’m going to be.’”

The way scientists talked about ephemeris at AMOS sounded like castaways on deserted islands pleading for water. As good as the radars and space cameras have gotten, they don’t tell you when and where a satellite is planning on moving.

“Our community has an ephemeris sharing problem,” Jonathan Herman, senior director of Starlink Constellation Engineering, said at his keynote address. “The No. 1 risk in LEO is not debris. It is instead that operators don’t know where other satellites are going.”

A visualization from COMSPOC, a company that tracks objects in space, shows a Chinese satellite crossing orbits.COMSPOC

Herman noted that Starlink satellites perform around 1,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers per day, all of which consume valuable fuel and decrease the lifespan of the satellites. That number of maneuvers was described to me as “horrendously high” in a previous interview. 

It’s a double-edged sword: Starlink does an exceptional job at avoiding objects in space, but the fact that they have to move so much makes it harder for other operators to know where its satellites are going to be. 

Still, almost everyone I talked to at AMOS spoke about Starlink as a responsible steward of space. If you wanted an example of reckless behavior in orbit, there were much easier targets. 

The geopolitical barrier

Not all of the technical problems involving satellite maneuvering are particularly complex. Herman, the Starlink director, said they could be solved in a few hours by getting everyone in a room together. The bigger hurdle is communication. 

“We may understand at an operator-to-operator level what the best practices are, and the Chinese operators may understand that, too,” Audrey Schaffer, senior VP of global policy and government strategy, said on a panel. “But the challenge that we have is that the Chinese government is uncomfortable with their operators going directly to other operators.”

Commercial and defense domains in space are deeply interwoven. (I heard some version of the sentence, “Space is a warfighting domain,” at least a dozen times at AMOS.) If there’s a space company that doesn’t rely on military money at all, I didn’t find it here. 

“Within the last 18 months, we’ve seen a lot more open discussion of the importance of defense funding,” said Ian Christensen, senior director of private sector programs at the Secure World Foundation. “There’s been a real pivot towards defense funding as the most stable and largest source of funding.”

That tension between military and civilian operations was woven through many of the conversations I had at AMOS. This development hasn’t come out of nowhere – Elon Musk said over a year ago that Ukraine’s “entire front line would collapse if I turned it off” — but you could feel AMOS’ attendees on both the military and commercial sides grappling with the balance in real-time. 

“Russia’s actions consider every vendor here a legitimate target based on their cooperation with the US government and governments of NATO,” Col. Jonathan Whitaker, chief of staff of NATO’s Combined Forces Space Component Command, said at a panel. “When you take that perspective, there’s really no safe harbor for a commercial company.”

The bottom line

I walked away from AMOS feeling simultaneously comforted and pessimistic. As one person put it to me, there are around 40,000 tracked objects, but the island of Maui alone has about 184,000 registered vehicles. 

The reality is more complicated — there are an estimated 1.2 million objects in orbit the size of a softball or smaller that aren’t tracked – but it’s a fair point. As Elon Musk is fond of saying, “Space is really big.”

“What I worry about is not so much the number of objects, which do make easier headlines,” said Swiney, the director at the Office of Space Commerce. “The much harder problem to solve is, how do you get someone on the phone if you’re not allowed to talk to them, or if you don’t even know what their phone number is in the first place?

“The technical problems are relatively easy to solve if we can get past the policy.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Joe Supan
						

						

							Senior Writer						
					

											

								

											Joe Supan is a senior writer for CNET covering home technology, broadband, and moving. Prior to joining CNET, Joe led MyMove's moving coverage and reported on broadband policy, the digital divide, and privacy issues for the broadband marketplace Allconnect. He has been featured as a guest columnist on Broadband Breakfast, and his work has been referenced by the Los Angeles Times, Forbes, National Geographic, Yahoo! Finance and more.

title: Gemini app for macOS adding send and read iMessage integration
snippet: Google’s latest update to the Gemini app for macOS readies local iMessage integration. This follows the app coming to Windows last week. more…
fullText:
Google’s latest update to the Gemini app for macOS readies local iMessage integration. This follows the app coming to Windows last week.

Gemini’s latest Connected App on the Mac is @messages to “Read, search, and send messages in Apple Messages.” Specifically, the integration can:

Send messages to contacts or phone numbers

Read recent conversations, unread messages, and search message history

This will aid context by being able to look up information from conversations. Example prompts include:

Send a message to John: “Running 5 minutes late!”

Show my recent messages from Sarah

Search Messages for dinner reservations

 In terms of limitations, Gemini cannot:

	

Manage group participant membership or change group chat photos

Schedule messages for future delivery or edit sent messages

Send file, photo, or media attachments (plain text messages only)

Send tapback reactions (love, like, dislike, laugh, emphasize, question)

Generate photos or images within automated task workflows

This integration appears in Settings > Connected Apps at the very bottom after updating to version 1.116.5.889 of Gemini for macOS. However, as of this afternoon, a server-side component appears to be missing, with @messages not yet recognized in the prompt box.

Recent updates to Gemini for macOS introduced a File Providers extension that shows “Add to Gemini” when you right-click on a file in Finder. This immediately adds the photo or document to the prompt box. It can be enabled in Settings > Extensions. Google also added Images, Videos, and Daily Brief to the side panel.

More on Gemini app:

title: Asus Googlebook shows off a big trackpad and plenty of ports in leaked images [Gallery]

title: Apple VP of hardware talks iPhone Duo durability, crease, hinge, and more
snippet: Apple’s new Vice President of Hardware Engineering, Tom Marieb, sat down with TechRadar for an interview all about iPhone Duo. Here’s what he said about iPhone Duo’s durability, the hinge, display crease, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new Vice President of Hardware Engineering, Tom Marieb, sat down with TechRadar for an interview all about iPhone Duo. Here’s what he said about iPhone Duo’s durability, the hinge, display crease, and more.

Apple put ‘blood, sweat, and tears’ into making iPhone Duo’s hinge durable and versatile, per interview

iPhone Duo will launch next month, bringing an all-new software experience to iPhone (see examples here) but also several hardware innovations.

Anyone interested in iPhone Duo may have questions about three key hardware features especially:

durability

the display crease (or lack thereof)

and the hinge

Today Axel Metz at TechRadar published quotes from an interview with Tom Marieb, the Apple’s new Vice President of Hardware Engineering. That’s the same role current CEO John Ternus once held.

The full interview is well worth a read, but here were some highlights.

When asked about the crease in iPhone Duo’s folding display, Marieb pointed to nano-texture as a great solution that he said would continue to minimize a visible crease even after extended use.

“Hold us accountable to that, please. The choice of a matte finish — apart from it being beautiful — is part of that equation. When you look at glossy displays, their specularity makes it very easy to pick up topology differences. That’s part of the reason we picked the matte finish — it’s not only beautiful in terms of preventing glare, but it’s also more forgiving of [hinge] changes over time.”

On the subject of iPhone Duo’s hinge, he said:

“We really worked on the torque profile very heavily, and that means changing a lot of the mechanical properties of the hinge to have it feel solid, like a high-end automobile’s car door, when you shut it. That was design intent, so people would have a feeling like, ‘Oh, it’s okay. This is well crafted, and it’s safe for me to use and not worry about it.’

And then, as you said, we have a lot of use cases where the Duo is [in a half-folded state]. And so we also had to think, ‘Can people interact with this [device] and not have it feel floppy?’ So getting those torque profiles right at both those ends, as well as in the middle — not having it feel like you’re pulling something open, and not feeling as if it’s floppy — we spent a lot of time optimizing that. So thank you for noticing, because a lot of blood, sweat, and tears went into that.”

Marieb also praised Ceramic Shield 2 as an incredible technology that makes third-party screen protectors unnecessary. He said, “Personally, when I see someone put a screen protector on their iPhone, it makes my skin crawl, because we work so hard to make beautiful front screens.”

You can read the full interview here on TechRadar.

title: Delayed Apple TV series ‘The Savant’ may finally air next year
snippet: If you cast your mind back to almost a year ago from today, Apple TV was about to launch a new series called The Savant starring Jessica Chastain … until it was pulled from the schedule at the last moment, in the wake of the assassination of political activist Charlie Kirk. Apple never gave an exact reason for cancelling the release, but promised it would release the series at a later date … more…
fullText:
If you cast your mind back to almost a year ago from today, Apple TV was about to launch a new series called The Savant starring Jessica Chastain … until it was pulled from the schedule at the last moment, in the wake of the assassination of political activist Charlie Kirk. 

Apple never gave an exact reason for cancelling the release, but promised it would release the series at a later date …

At the time, star Jessica Chastain made a statement to say that she was ‘not aligned’ with Apple’s decision to postpone the show’s premiere.

Nevertheless, here we are a year later, and The Savant has still not come out. In fact, if you look up the series in the Apple TV app, the page still reads “coming at a later date” and has an awkwardly outdated ‘2025’ year label. 

However, Variety reports today that the streamer has finally put the series back on its slate, with a release date scheduled for spring 2027.

The spring launch would aim to put the series in prime contention for the next Emmy awards season, which means Apple would want to get all episodes aired sometime before the cutoff date of May 31, 2027.

Of course, Apple could decide to once again delay the release when we get closer to springtime. Whatever Chastain’s thoughts are on how The Savant has been handled, the actress has continued to work with Apple on other upcoming projects, including starring in ‘The Dealer’ with Adam Driver, and alongside Ben Stiller in ‘The Off Weeks’.

title: iFixit tears down iPhone 18 Pro, explores variable aperture, finds concerning repair issue
snippet: iFixit has published its traditional teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, which shows the variable aperture mechanism up close and explores a potential issue involving display repairs. Watch it below. more…
fullText:
iFixit has published its traditional teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, which shows the variable aperture mechanism up close and explores a potential issue involving display repairs. Watch it below.

iFixit worries about possible display frame issue

iFixit’s teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro is now live, exploring not just the variable aperture, this year’s biggest camera upgrade, but also the device’s larger vapor chamber, the new under-display Face ID camera, and more.

When it comes to the variable aperture mechanism, iFixit notes that its six tiny blades are controlled by electromagnets, much like the optical image stabilization system, though the two mechanisms operate independently.

During the teardown, one of the tiny aperture blades flew out as iFixit dismantled the lens stack, underscoring how impractical a component-level repair would be. The group says that if the aperture gets stuck, it would likely require replacing the entire main camera assembly.

Another highlight of the new iPhone 18 Pro is its under-display Face ID infrared camera. For this year’s Pro devices, Apple moved the infrared camera beneath the display, while keeping the selfie camera and IR dot projector within the smaller Dynamic Island.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that Apple hides the relocated infrared camera by removing every other row of pixels above the sensor. iFixit notes that the effect fades toward the edges, and that there is an IR-pass filter beneath the OLED layer to block visible light.

Interestingly, the filter doesn’t extend all the way to the edge of the opening, creating what iFixit describes as an “eclipse effect” under certain microscope settings.

As for the iPhone 18 Pro’s bigger vapor chamber, the teardown offers a closer look at Apple’s redesigned cooling architecture.

As the company explained during its “Surprise and Shine” event, the A20 Pro uses a new package that places the silicon die side-by-side with the memory, removing the latter from the SoC’s thermal path and allowing the chip to connect directly to the vapor chamber. Apple also said the new vapor chamber has three times the surface area of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro.

iFixit’s teardown lets us see that setup up close, including the thermal material that presses the A20 Pro directly against the vapor chamber and the chamber itself extending across much of the phone’s body.

Now for the concerning part: iFixit says the plastic frame around the display was damaged on three of the four iPhones its team opened.

While the group notes that other iPhone 18 Pro teardowns haven’t encountered the same issue, and that Apple has been using this same plastic frame since the iPhone 15 Pro, it says it’s too early to tell whether this was an anomaly or a broader repairability concern.

iFixit also suggests that the device’s improved thermal system may be drawing heat away from the display as the heating pad tries to soften the adhesive.

Be that as it may, in practice, as iFixIt explains in the video, a cracked frame means the display may no longer sit perfectly flush after reassembly, and could compromise the phone’s water resistance.

Add to that the fact that some components remain difficult to reach, particularly the USB-C port, which iFixit says requires removing much of the phone’s internals to replace, and DIY repairs of the iPhone 18 Pro may prove challenging depending on which component needs replacing.

All in all, iFixit says the iPhone 18 Pro carries over many of the same repairability strengths and weaknesses as last year’s model, including the glue-free battery tray and modular camera assemblies, but also the need to enter through the display for most major repairs.

For now, the group has given both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max a provisional repairability score of 7 out of 10 as it waits for parts, conducts more tests, and watches whether the display frame issue proves widespread.

title: Pixel Now Playing update brings interface tweaks & notifications [U]
snippet: The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks. more…
fullText:
The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks.

Update 9/17: Following a server-side update, Now Playing 2026.08.27x and Android System Intelligence C.6 reintroduces Recognized Music Notifications. These silent alerts let you see what’s playing without having to open the app or checking the Quick Settings Tile. Expanding the notification lets you jump to the History tab and favorite songs.

Enabled by default, you can disable them in Now Playing Settings > Notifications.

Original 9/2: When tapping on an identified song’s three-dot button, Now Playing slides up a bottom sheet. This replaces the floating menu and is better for one-handed navigation.

	

You’ll see track information with side-by-side buttons for Share, Add to favorites, and Remove from history. This is followed by a button to play the song and any shortcuts specific to your connected music service.

Meanwhile, the Favorites tab now includes dates and times like the History feed. There are also icon and spacing tweaks in Now Playing Settings.

The redesigned Now Playing launched in March, while Google in April reintroduced the “Tap to see what’s playing” shortcut on the lockscreen.

Version 2026.08.27.x of Pixel Now Playing is widely rolling out via the Google Play Store.

This follows last month’s updates to Pixel Journal that added more tools and Screenshots (extra filter options), as well as new icons for Google Calculator, Clock, Pixel Magnifier, Recorder, and Weather.

snippet: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max bring several changes to the Main camera and iOS Camera app, and photographer Austin Mann has just published a great review of everything new. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max bring several changes to the Main camera and iOS Camera app, and photographer Austin Mann has just published a great review of everything new.

Austin Mann publishes in-depth review of iPhone 18 Pro camera upgrades

Credit: Austin Mann using iPhone 18 Pro

Every year, photographer Austin Mann puts out an in-depth review of the iPhone’s new camera features—complete with plenty of photos, of course.

Mann’s review of the iPhone 18 Pro camera upgrades was published today. I highly recommend checking it out for an overview of the new features and sampling of photos they enable.

On the new variable aperture feature, Mann says:

I recommend leaving your aperture in Auto. The camera is very, very good at picking the best aperture for the scene, and it’s usually better at it than me. Inside at dinner? f/1.48, auto-selected. Outside with plenty of light and depth? It picks a higher f-stop to keep everything in focus.

He shares beautiful examples of iPhone 18 Pro’s new wider aperture capturing the Colorado sky at night.

Credit: Austin Mann using iPhone 18 Pro

Regarding the new Pro controls that are exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Mann was especially excited to find Manual Focus:

One of the most-asked-for features by photographers has been the ability to separate exposure and focus, and now we can! All you do is set your focus manually (with focus peaking that works quite well!) and then tap where you want to expose.

In covering Photographic Styles 3, other reviewers like Tyler Stalman have highlighted the ability to create a film-like look with your photos. Mann echoes this and provides the following tips for the best film effect:

“Shoot dark, like -1.0, and shoot wide open at f/1.48. Use manual focus, which will make the image slightly softer (which is OK!).”

“Shoot HEIF so you can apply Photographic Styles.”

“Then in post, on the D-Pad, put the dot in the very lower right. This reduces the tone-mapping (aka the HDR look) and crunches your shadows and blows your highlights.”

“You can dial back the Film effect to reduce halation, which sometimes goes a bit overboard.”

You can watch Austin Mann’s video review below.

Also covered in Mann’s full review are features like Focus Tracking, Apple Reference Image, 4K time-lapse, and more.

Check out Austin Mann’s full iPhone 18 Pro camera review here.

title: Apple TV just dropped trailers for two upcoming premieres
snippet: Apple TV just kicked off a new season of Slow Horses, and plenty more premieres are coming soon, including a new movie and returning show that just got new trailers. more…
fullText:
Apple TV just kicked off a new season of Slow Horses, and plenty more premieres are coming soon, including a new movie and returning show that just got new trailers.

#1: Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars (season 2)

Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars is a culinary docuseries that first debuted last fall and has a new season coming very soon.

If you’re into The Bear, but want a real-world, nonfiction version of the show, Knife Edge might be the perfect fit. Its first season scored a BAFTA nomination for excellence in “Factual Entertainment.”

Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars returns next Friday, September 25 for season 2.

Here’s Apple’s summary of the show, followed by its trailer:

Across season two, “Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars” follows 16 restaurants at pivotal moments in their journeys: A chef and his family risk everything to put a tiny island on Michelin’s map. Two generations of a legendary culinary family pursue recognition on their own terms. Two chefs voluntarily give up their Star when they open a new restaurant and have just 52 days to win it back. One sandwich shop transforms into a fine dining restaurant each night, while a young couple seeks to put Filipino cuisine at the center of one of America’s most competitive dining scenes. Their circumstances could hardly be more different, yet each faces the same uncertainty: When Michelin makes its decision, will everything they have strived for be enough?

#2: Tenzing

Apple Original Films has a pair of movies coming this fall that have big award ambitions. The first of those titles is Tenzing.

The film hails from award-winning director Jennifer Peedom and stars Genden Phuntsok, Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe, Caitríona Balfe, Thinley Lhamo, and Tenzin Dalha.

Tenzing hits select theaters on Friday, October 9 before streaming October 16 on Apple TV.

Here’s the plot summary, followed by the trailer:

Based on true events, “Tenzing” chronicles the little-known story of Tenzing Norgay (Phuntsok), a gifted Himalayan climber who, alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary (Hiddleston), became the first to summit Mount Everest. Encouraged by his wife, Dawa (Lhamo), Tenzing finds an ally in expedition secretary Jill Henderson (Balfe). Together, they persuade Colonel John Hunt (Dafoe) that Tenzing belongs on the British climbing team, rather than merely serving it. Where Western climbers see “Everest” as something to be conquered, Tenzing reveres “Chomolungma” as the sacred mother goddess. What follows is an ascent defined as much by the tensions between backgrounds, classes and competing ambitions as by the perils of the mountain itself. But high above the world, empire, rank and aspiration fall away, leaving two outsiders bound by mutual respect and trust — and for Tenzing, the fulfillment of both a lifelong dream and a spiritual calling.

title: Google rolling out September 2026 update for Pixel Watch 2, 3, & 4
snippet: As part of the September 2026 Feature Drop, Google today is rolling out a Wear OS update to the Pixel Watch 2, 3, and 4. more…
fullText:
As part of the September 2026 Feature Drop, Google today is rolling out a Wear OS update to the Pixel Watch 2, 3, and 4.

Google shared the following build numbers this afternoon, but the factory and OTA images are not yet live:

Pixel Watch 3 & 4: CP3A.260905.002

Pixel Watch 2: CP3A.260905.002.E1

All watches (Pixel Watch 2 and up) are receiving “Gemini Personalization” that leverages both your past conversations and connected Google apps (Gmail, Calendar, Search, YouTube, and Photos) for more personalized responses. This is “powered by an offline user profile and real-time online retrieval working together.” 

Like on the web and mobile, Personalization allows for prompts like “What’s on my calendar today” and “Find the tracking number in my email.”

	

Meanwhile, users of the Pixel Watch 3 and newer can now: 

Double pinch to open At a Glance from watch face 

Double pinch to open notification center from watch face 

Double pinch to scroll through Gemini response

Double pinch to scroll through cards in Wallet app

Double pinch to scroll through your workout metrics

Double pinch to toggle between Google Maps views

Double pinch to manage Recorder app

Wrist turn gesture as universal back navigation

The Pixel Watch 4 and newer benefit from improved raise-to-talk performance thanks to an updated gesture model. 

“General bug fixes and improvements” is the final item on the changelog.

title: Gmail adds ‘Copy code’ shortcut for 2FA on Android & iOS
snippet: After rolling out Live search and chat earlier this month, Gmail now has a useful “Copy code” button for 2FA on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
After rolling out Live search and chat earlier this month, Gmail now has a useful “Copy code” button for 2FA on Android and iOS.

Instead of having to open an email to select and copy the two-factor authentication code, Gmail now shows a shortcut directly in your inbox. The pill-shaped “Copy code 000000” button appears below the subject line, like the previews for images, documents, and other attachments.

Tapping the button simply adds the code to your clipboard for a quick paste in the designated app. 

We’ve seen it work for store and banking emails in our brief testing today. It’s a nice quality-of-life addition.

	

The Copy code button is appearing in Gmail for Android (version 2026.09.07.x) and iOS (6.0.260907), but not on the web. This shortcut would also be useful in email notifications on Android.

title: Control Resonant Builds on Remedy’s Weird Mythos, but Bleeds It Over an Open World
snippet: Mundane world activities dilute the signature X-Files delight of Control, but when it hits, it hits.
fullText:
Remedy Entertainment has proved time and again that its distinctive blend of tone, atmosphere, action and surprise resonates with players — so much so that its best games are remembered for their highs and forgiven for their flaws. It’s easy to forget that 2019’s Control had uneven difficulty and some rote bosses that rubbed some gamers the wrong way when its strong, distinct storytelling captivated them throughout. The same was true of 2023’s Alan Wake II, which blended strangeness and character-driven storytelling so effectively that its difficulty spikes were easy to overlook.

Which is why the follow-up to Control, titled Control Resonant, will probably find its way into gamers’ hearts despite taking some of the wrong lessons from Remedy’s earlier games. Nowhere else will you find an experience quite like Resonant, even if the studio’s magic feels somewhat diluted from lunging after mainstream gameplay elements that, quite frankly, aren’t why people play a Remedy game. 

There’s a throughline of strong, novel storytelling that still runs through — and shines in — Resonant. After the new director of the Federal Bureau of Control, Jesse Faden, carved a path through the extradimensional Hiss invasion to save her brother, Dylan, at the end of 2019’s Control, her victories dried up. Seven years into the stalemate, Jesse bids her brother goodbye and plunges a powerful weapon into him. When he wakes, the Hiss have broken out of the FBC’s headquarters to possess all of Manhattan — and, in turn, the world.

That’s where Resonant begins, with a promise that Dylan’s attempt to redeem his past Hiss-possessed sins will lead to a cornucopia of weird adventures that made Control so special — but this time, on a city-wide scale. He grabs a radio off an FBC grunt and links up with Zoe, a field squad leader brigadiered into handling New York City’s messy streets after everyone senior has been eliminated. Learning who Dylan is, she cautiously holds his leash, sending him on missions as she struggles to believe he’s thrown off the yoke of destruction.

For the record, so does Dylan, but it doesn’t make it easier to stomach the abuse hurled at him by FBC agents bringing up their many dead colleagues. In an early story mission deep into a Hiss-controlled skyscraper, Dylan is periodically overwhelmed by memories of possession, even forced to relive the murderous early days when the FBC’s HQ, the Oldest House, was overcome by the malevolent and monstrous Hiss. Fighting through his fears, he saves a prominent FBC chief thought lost, who still treats him with disdain. Dylan’s uncertain redemptive march is, pardon the pun, one of the most resonant themes of the game.

It’s unfortunate that it took me 10 hours of fumbling about in the rest of the open world to reach that point. Shortly after starting the game, players are turned loose in a few connected Manhattan neighborhoods with little indication of what will and won’t be signature Remedy experiences. It’s so easy to get lost in the routine hack-and-slash gameplay that I started worrying that the game lacked the studio’s signature juice.

Resonant’s Manhattan looks much like any generic American city.Remedy Entertainment/Screenshot by CNET

Mucking through a city that doesn’t feel much like Manhattan

When players excitedly fired up 2014’s BioWare fantasy adventure Dragon Age: Inquisition, they quickly got mired in the opening area, lost and baffled that their beloved series might have been subsumed into a mundane open-world adventure. Advice spread through the game’s community like wildfire: Leave the Hinterlands opening area and you’ll reach the real game.

That recommendation regrettably applies to Resonant. Remedy isn’t too keen on holding players’ hands through its games, and at a time when vocal players condemn overprescribed direction (such as the infamous yellow paint), it’s understandable that Resonant’s developers would leave players to their own devices. The game points them toward a list of goals and lets them take the lead.

But most of the early-game goals involve delving into dungeons tucked into the corners of vast open-world areas populated by roaming squads of Hiss. According to the story, this is Manhattan, but its stretches of streets and rooftops feel generic, resembling the sleepy apartment blocks of Brooklyn south of Prospect Heights more than the bustling heart of America’s most iconic city. Remedy smartly avoided resorting to instantly recognizable landmarks and iconic buildings, but that meant the only things that reminded me of my eight years in NYC were the laundromats and pseudo-bodegas I ducked into for item chests.

This may not be any Manhattan I recognize, but I sure want to explore it.Remedy Entertainment/Screenshot by CNET

The game’s areas that are most striking are the ones that could be in any city, and even the sidequests don’t make it feel like any particular place. Resonant’s Manhattan has the most identity when it’s warped by the Hiss or a new force called the Patterning, which significantly alters the city’s geometry. Here, at least, Remedy gets to flex its design muscles with some radically fun, distorted topography.

One thing Remedy gets right is that New York City is perpetually under construction, using scaffolding as diegetic platforms for gaining height and soaring over gray-brown buildings. Temporary flight returns from Control, and it’s still a hoot to awkwardly hurl yourself at enemies and whack them with the Aberrant, Dylan’s shape-shifting Altered Item. Unlike Control’s gun-based combat, Dylan’s weapon is melee-only, and can take the form of a wide reaper’s scythe to hit multiple enemies or a pair of daggers for quick attacks. But gathering upgrade materials to build out your arsenal is a slow process, which left me with a single set of attacks for hours and hours. (Remedy seems to like this miserly upgrade pace, which was very evident in its ill-fated multiplayer experiment, FBC: Firebreak.)

Remedy Entertainment/Screenshot by CNET

Oddly, the Aberrant’s imagery might be the most strikingly familiar to New Yorkers: In the subspace where Dylan manages his powers and upgrades, the weapon is massively enlarged into a steel I-beam driven through the concrete ground, evoking memories of the wreckage of 9/11.

And boy, will you get to know your arsenal, as every area and lull between story sequences is packed with combat against similar Hiss enemies — or, later, infectious Mold creatures. Like most of Remedy’s games, it becomes the price of entry as you progress. Bosses are deliciously designed — early on, you fight a giant sculpted head; later, a titanic magma creature in a furnace — but inconsistently challenging. I was able to beat the latter only after boosting my stats enough to wear it down.

Remedy Entertainment/Screenshot by CNET

The best of Remedy isn’t in the open world

Remedy’s Manhattan looks flatly normal in some areas, while others bend in on themselves, as in the film Inception. These Gravityland sections are fun places to use the game’s other major movement mechanic: jumping around while reorienting yourself to walls and ceilings. But they also show how little even this novelty does for me. The best parts of the game — and perhaps every Remedy game — are indoors.

There’s a reason players fell in love with Control’s Oldest House, a relic outside of time with brutalist concrete and groovy 1960s style that promised and evoked so much mystery, from its heights to its depths. I’ve played around 18 hours of Resonant, and only now — delving deep into a new region underground filled with floating block structures over a potent abyss — have I found an area that fills me with the wonder I felt wandering around the first game. It’s no surprise that these indoor areas are riddled with the stunning light, shadows and color that Remedy expertly deploys to set stark moods.

Remedy Entertainment/Screenshot by CNET

It’s admirable that Remedy would try applying its formula to the open world, but these areas are weaker, their sense of warped weirdness diluted by daylight and recognizable mundanity. The story-heavy missions within enclosed areas far better showcase Remedy’s blend of action and environment. In one standout sequence, Dylan is dropped into a sinkhole atop a diving bell, with Zoe keeping in touch over a PA system. He must fight through a Gravityland-warped apartment complex and defeat a boss at the bottom, only for the bell to be accidentally yanked away. Fighting despair as Zoe’s frantic calls fragment over dimensional interference, Dylan hears a song she plays over the PA, and he follows it through a dizzying stretch of rooms to escape. 

This — this is the kind of sequence that sticks in players’ minds, combining character arcs, action, surrealism and a new yet graspable environmental logic that bends the brain in the best way. It doubles as a great needle drop, like all of Remedy’s greatest sequences. (The studio was so confident in this section that it was part of Resonant’s Summer Game Fest demo.)

Remedy Entertainment/Screenshot by CNET

It’s easy to forget that Remedy itself began with games exploring New York City, but the Max Payne series was intentionally set in a version of NYC riddled with rain, crime and drama. So far in my time with the game, Resonant’s best parts aren’t set in subways, rooftops or skyscrapers; they’re in the bizarre, altered corners that could be anywhere, really. Anywhere you happen to fall through the cracks of normalcy and realize the world is larger, stranger and more dangerous than you thought.

There’s a version of Resonant that might have perfectly synthesized this into the Big Apple, but I (and many other gamers, I’m betting) will be willing to trudge through missteps exploring a game unlike any other, relishing the moments where Remedy swings for the fences — and knocks it out of the park.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile						
					

											

								

											David Lumb is a managing editor for the mobile team, covering mobile and gaming spaces. Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. title: Every single new feature in Android 17 QPR1 [Video]
snippet: Get ready, Android 17 QPR1 is now available, and it might be a refresh that hardware holdouts hope is going to give them some great new features – here is everything new. more…
fullText:
Get ready, Android 17 QPR1 is now available, and it might be a refresh that hardware holdouts hope is going to give them some great new features – here is everything new.

Just a few weeks after the Pixel 11 started shipping, we now have a fresh update to install and run on your new phone, or any device from the Pixel 6 through to the newest additions. We are not getting huge changes here, just a few tweaks, some more refinements, mostly quality of life changes.

If you want more, the Pixel Drop for September 2026 adds a little more flavor to what is, in all honesty, a very small update by the standards of Quarterly Platform Releases. As noted, most of the new functionality is very minimal at best or not notable at worst. You’ll probably notice that this update is heavily weighted toward cosmetic changes. That’s mostly just a symptom of Android hitting a bit of a functionality ceiling as of late.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

UI changes

Core user interface changes are part and parcel of any Android update, as things get tweaked and tuned to help improve the cohesion of specific sections and subsections. All UI changes we have tracked relate to commonly used areas and features within Android 17 QPR1, with changes over the previous base Android 17 and 16 builds and releases noted.

Lockscreen animation slide-ins improved

Google has tuned one of the key lockscreen UI portions with a vastly improved slide-in animation for media player controls while your phone is locked. When you have something playing, and your phone is locked, tapping the power button or the screen causes the media player UI to slide up into view rather than being static on your display.

It’s super clean and gives this already fun section just a little more life per Material 3 Expressive’s aim for more playful UI interactions.

Pixel Search settings in App List settings

Although live on the Pixel 11, older Pixels will get access to the new Pixel Search settings option within App list settings. This gives you options for the search bar at the top of the App drawer, so you can tune the experience to show suggestions, apps, and full web search, and adjust whether the keyboard appears automatically.

Stashed media player in Quick Settings

If you have multiple media apps open or are using multiple at the same time, Android 17 QPR1 now stashes these within the Quick Settings panel so you are able to switch quickly while still making it easy to manage one at a time. This change is also present on the lockscreen.

Usability changes

Android 17 QPR1 includes a host of usability enhancements aimed at making everyday device interactions smoother and more intuitive. This section details these core changes to the Android 17 QPR1 experience, which may also include some new functionalities.

Predictive back gesture in Quick Settings

Predictive back or a close approximation is coming to the Quick Setting panel, as you’ll get a visual indicator of what will happen when using back gestures. Instead of just minimizing, you’ll see the notifications appear when fully expanded (if there are any). Then, going back once more will show the homescreen before you release the gesture.

This is a better implementation than in previous versions, as the section would just collapse with no indication of where you’d end up.

Keyboard QS tile

Android 17 QPR1 has a new Keyboard tile that you can add to Quick Settings. If you add and activate it, it gives you the pop-up menu for your installed keyboards, allowing you to quickly switch anywhere within your device system. Long pressing opens up the Keyboard apps section and allows you to enable or disable any installed apps. If you have multiple keyboard applications, this might be a really neat, quick tool to switch when required.

New mobile data pop-up

Easily one of the best new features in Android 17 QPR1 is the ability to dismiss the annoying “Turn on mobile data” pop-up that usually appears every time you want to make a change. When you turn mobile data off and then re-enable it, there’s a new checkbox labeled “Do not ask me again,” so you won’t keep getting prompted to turn on mobile data if you have disabled it momentarily.

Some applications with multiple actions and shortcuts offer split panels to reduce on-screen clutter – especially on smaller displays. When you long-press an app icon such as Pocket Casts, the default app actions, including widgets, remove, app info, pause, and bubble, will be visible. A new “Shortcuts” toggle lets you tap to access quick in-app shortcuts and add them to your homescreen. Not all apps will have these options.

Screen recording adjustments

In Android 17 QPR1, Google has adjusted the menu so that the last-used app is now the default option, and the dropdown menu starts with “single app” selected. If you were to tap “start” immediately, the most recent app would be selected and recorded. Previously, this defaulted to “Entire Screen.”

Cosmetic changes

Alongside features, Android 17 QPR1 focuses on some cosmetic or visual changes to the experience you’ll have with your Pixel phone. Most are merely updates to areas that may have been overlooked or recently added in previous software versions.

New QS edit tile icon

If you want to edit your Quick Settings tiles, there is a new icon that combines the pencil icon with some tiles to show you how the enhanced system works.

When you view sections in Settings, the spacing increases to pre-Android 17 levels, making things feel less cramped, albeit with fewer options on screen. You’ll have to scroll a little more.

Gemini Intelligence boot logo

We’re not actually sure how widespread this is, given that Gemini Intelligence isn’t technically expected to come to older Pixel phones now. Some may see the Gemini Intelligence logo when rebooting or powering on their devices, but only on the Pixel 10 and newer. It’s already live on Pixel 11 devices.

Many of the pop-up menus on your Pixel will be smaller with Android 17 QPR1. This is prominent with the Wallpaper and style pop-up and some of the mini menus.

New app icons

Google has updated the entire suite of default app icons, including Settings and various other first-party apps like Clock, Calculator, and Recorder, to fit the new “Pixel style.” 

Improved animations

Some further attention has been paid to animations added over the last couple of years, with even more bounce when using Quick Settings. Tiles respond to slide speed, exhibiting overshoot and easing back into position. Some other animations have a little more bounce, but it’s most visible here.

Increased system blur

Not to be confused with Liquid Glass, Google’s system blur effect is more prominent in more areas with marginally more glassy visuals in the app drawer, volume slider sidebar, the power menu, and app pop-ups. It’s not completely frosted, but has increased opacity.

App notification dot visual update

If you have enabled notification dots in Android 17 QPR1, you will see a new Dynamic Color-styled outline that helps the dot stand out from icons.

title: Google just shared these fun Pixel 11 blueprint wallpapers [Gallery]
snippet: Google has shared some new blueprint-style wallpapers for the Pixel 11 series, and they look pretty awesome. more…
fullText:
Google has shared some new blueprint-style wallpapers for the Pixel 11 series, and they look pretty awesome.

Shared through the Google Japan account on Twitter/X, two blueprint-style wallpapers show off the internals of Google’s new phones from the front or the back. 

The front-facing view can line up directly with the frame and shows parts of the phone such as the front-facing camera, vapor chamber cooling, USB-C port, speaker, and various other components.

The rear-facing view shows the camera module, battery, and many other parts of the device. Notably, though, you have to crop this one in a bit further as, being displayed on the main screen, the buttons would end up being on the wrong side.

	

Either way, it’s a fun wallpaper set from Google, and not the first time the company has offered something like this. Back in 2023, some Pixel 7 Pro teardown images made for a really cool wallpaper, and Google also shared 25-year anniversary graphics that could be used as wallpapers that same year.

title: Apple showcases iPhone 18 Pro camera with new ‘What Holds Us’ photography exhibition
snippet: Apple is holding a new photography exhibition in New York City this weekend to showcase the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is holding a new photography exhibition in New York City this weekend to showcase the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Here are the details.

’Images that speak to presence as both a state of mind and a way of being’

If you are in the New York area this weekend, Apple is opening a new photography exhibition featuring original work shot entirely on the iPhone 18 Pro.

Running from September 18 through September 20 at 456 West 18th Street in New York City, Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibition will feature work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity,” the company says.

The exhibition was curated by Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, and is meant to showcase the range of creative possibilities enabled by the iPhone 18 Pro’s new camera system, including its variable aperture.

According to Apple, Chin’s work focuses on the Bugaboo Mountains in British Columbia, where he photographed climbers against the surrounding landscape. His images range from tight close-ups to wide panoramas and action shots.

Here’s Chin:

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. (…) I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Jack Davison went for a more intimate approach, photographing people interacting with clay and chalk inside a former sugar warehouse in London.

Commenting on the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera, he said:

“I genuinely was blown away by the camera on iPhone 18 Pro. (…) There was something about the quality of the imagery that felt like a huge leap. Not just from a technical standpoint, but in its ability to create more artistic and surreal images. That really surprised me. The ability to switch between lenses, use slower shutters, and shoot RAW made it such a potent package.”

As for Alex Prager, she created large-scale crowd scenes on a soundstage in Los Angeles, combining wide overhead shots with tighter portraits and details.

Here’s Prager on what she took away from the experience:

“Photography has changed a lot, and this particular camera is more like a video stream, in essence, which also shapes how we approach images today — more like video with higher output in our photo albums and on social media. (…). It was exciting for me to think about all of this while harking back to a timeless crowd winding down from a celebration.”

title: Here’s everything new in Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 [Gallery]
snippet: Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 is rolling out today to continue the development cycle ahead of the stable December launch. more…
fullText:
Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 is rolling out today to continue the development cycle ahead of the stable December launch.

Over the coming hours, we’ll dive into all of Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5’s new features and every single change. (The newest updates will be at the top of this list. Be sure to check back often and tell us what you find in the comments below.) Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 screenshots appear on the left and Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 on the right.

If you want to quickly install Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 on your compatible Pixel 6a, Pixel 7, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel Tablet, Pixel Fold, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 10a, Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold be sure to check out our step-by-step guide.

Updating…

	

2x Proactive Assistance

On the Pixel 10 and 11 series, we’re seeing a second “Proactive Assistance” menu appear in Settings. The original (as debuted on the Pixel 11) is near the bottom of the list with a blue icon, while the second appears higher with a yellow light bulb icon. Their descriptions are similar, but not identical. The explicit mention of Gemini is the difference.

Blue: “Get personalized suggestions from Gemini at the right time”

Yellow: “Personalized suggestions at the right time”

Blue (original) vs. yellow (QPR2)

From the explanations, both settings pages appear to reference the same capability. Toggling off the original (blue) menu also disables the new switch (yellow).

However, the new menu has a “Use app content for suggestions” page that lets you enable/disable “which apps can share screen content and notifications with Proactive Assistance for suggestions.” There’s also a shortcut to the “Default digital assistant app” page.

This change was first introduced on the Pixel 11 series

Quick Settings: New Audio streams Tile + Layout customization removed

Unclear if layout customization will return before the final QPR2 release, or if Google decided to not proceed with the capability

Additionally, Voice broadcast Tile now under Connectivity instead of system apps

Fixes

Changing a Bluetooth device type in settings failed to update its icon visually. (Issue #516071134)

A system stability issue that caused unexpected device reboots during continuous UI scrolling in media-heavy applications. (Issue #544291113)

Pressing hardware volume buttons while casting media prevented the system volume slider UI from displaying. (Issue #548145018)

Fixed a text-rendering issue that caused unexpected background highlights to appear when typing in search fields, and resolved a navigation routing issue that prevented Private Space from unlocking correctly. (Issue #548285596)

Enhanced HDR mode remained enabled despite being turned off in user settings. (Issue #547457910)

Launching Google Wallet via the power button shortcut caused the touchscreen to become unresponsive. (Issue #549758084)

Camera crashes during panorama processing. (Issue #551069625)

Bluetooth audio experiences noise and distortion after completing or answering a call. (Issue #541684282)
